## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One
## 1. Ekaka Nipāta
## 1. Apaṇṇaka Vagga
## 1. Apaṇṇaka Jātaka
Some wise people take the certain cause which is the means of liberation from suffering and the realization of true welfare; speculators speak of the second (false) cause. A wise person, knowing the benefit and harm in these two causes, should take only that certain (apaṇṇaka) cause which leads to liberation from suffering.

## Apaṇṇaka Jātaka, the First.

## 2. Vaṇṇupatha Jātaka
Just as those who are untiring, when digging in the desert, obtain water in that sandy plain; even so the sage, endowed with the power of effort, should obtain the peace of the heart (Nibbāna) by practicing without laziness.

## Vaṇṇupatha Jātaka, the Second.
2:
## 3. Serivavāṇija Jātaka
If in this Dispensation you fail to attain the path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), which is the mark of the righteous, you will grieve for a long time, just as this foolish trinket-seller named Seriva grieved repeatedly.

## Serivavāṇija Jātaka, the Third.

## 4. Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka
A wise and discerning person, skilled in the means of trade, establishes himself by generating much wealth and attendants from a small capital, just as one blows a small fire into a great heap of flames.

## Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka, the Fourth.

## 5. Taṇḍulanāḷi Jātaka
O Great King, tell me, how much is this measure of rice worth for the price of horses? This measure of rice is indeed worth the city of Bārāṇasī, including its inner and outer parts.

## Taṇḍulanāḷi Jātaka, the Fifth.

## 6. Devadhamma Jātaka
Those who are endowed with shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) in the world, who are established in the pure wholesome Dhamma, and who are peaceful and righteous, are called those who possess the 'Divine Dhamma' (Devadhamma).

## Devadhamma Jātaka, the Sixth.

## 7. Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka
O Great King, ruler of men, I am your son; please nourish me. Your Majesty nourishes even others; why do you not nourish me, who am your own true offspring?

## Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka, the Seventh.
3:
## 8. Gāmaṇi Jātaka
Even for those who do not hurry (and are patient), the desired benefit will surely be fulfilled. Gāmaṇi, know thus that I am one whose holy life has matured.

## Gāmaṇi Jātaka, the Eighth.

## 9. Maghadeva Jātaka
These grey hairs that have grown on my head and take away my youth have appeared. These grey hairs are divine messengers; it is indeed the time for my renunciation.

## Maghadeva Jātaka, the Ninth.

## 10. Sukhavihāri Jātaka
He whom others need not guard, and who does not need to guard others—O King, that person, being indifferent to sensual pleasures, truly sleeps in happiness.

## Sukhavihāri Jātaka, the Tenth.

## 1. Apaṇṇaka Vagga
The summary (uddāna) of that group is:
The noble Apaṇṇaka Jātaka, Vaṇṇupatha Jātaka, Serivavāṇija Jātaka, the wise Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka, Taṇḍulanāḷika Jātaka, Devadhamma Jātaka endowed with hiri and ottappa, the noble son Kaṭṭhavāhana Jātaka, Gāmaṇi Jātaka, Maghadeva Jātaka, and the Sukhavihāri Jātaka beginning with "He whom others need not guard"—these are the ten.

## 2. Sīla Vagga

## 11. Lakkhaṇamiga Jātaka
Benefit comes to those who have good conduct and virtue, and are endowed with the practice of hospitality. Look at the deer Lakkhaṇa approaching, surrounded by a host of kinsmen. Then look at this deer Kāḷa, who is greatly deprived of kinsmen (coming alone).

## Lakkhaṇamiga Jātaka, the First.
4:
## 12. Nigrodhamiga Jātaka
12. One who desires welfare should associate only with the Nigrodha deer; one should not dwell with the Sākha deer. Death in the presence of the Nigrodha deer-king is better than life in the presence of the Sākha deer-king.

## Nigrodhamiga Jātaka, the Second.

## 13. Kaṇḍi Jātaka
13. Abominable is the man with the piercing arrow who shoots severely. Abominable is that country where a woman is the leader. Also cursed are those beings who have fallen under the power of women.

## Kaṇḍi Jātaka, the Third.

## 14. ဝါတမိဂဇာတကံ
14. It is said that in the world there is nothing more evil than tastes (cravings). Taste is more evil than dwellings or friends. Sañjaya, the gardener, brought the wind-deer named Vātāmiga, who lived in the forest, under his power by means of tastes.

## Vātāmiga Jātaka, the Fourth.

## 15. ခရာဒိယဇာတကံ
15. Kharādiya, I no longer strive to discipline that deer who has eight hooves, whose horns are crooked at the base and tip, and who has exceeded seven periods of instruction and is difficult to discipline.

## Kharādiya Jātaka, the Fifth.

I have taught him the deer-guile by which, breathing on the ground with one nostril pressed to the earth, he can deceive and overcome the hunter through the six basic arts. ## Tipallatthamiga Jātaka, the Sixth. ## 17. The summary of that chapter is:
Lakkhaṇa Jātaka, Sākha Jātaka, Sirī Jātaka, Cūḷanandiya Jātaka, Punappuna Jātaka, Kiratthi Jātaka, Rasehi (Dummedha) Jātaka, Kharādiya Jātaka, Atibhoti (Itthi) Jātaka, Māluta Jātaka, and Naḷapāna Jātaka—these are the ten.

## 3. Kuruṅgavagga

## 21. Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka

O Sepaṇṇi tree, the deer has understood the reason why you cause the fruit to fall in such a scattered manner.
I shall go to another tree; I no longer delight in your fruit.

## Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka, the First.

## 22. Kukkura Jātaka

O Great King, those dogs that are reared in the royal palace, born in the royal house, and endowed with beauty and strength—
Those dogs are not to be killed, yet we are the ones to be killed.
This is not a slaughter pertaining to all dogs; it is only a slaughter of the weak.

## Kukkura Jātaka, the Second.

## 23. Gojānīya Jātaka

O Charioteer, though I am lying on my side, having been pierced by arrows and suffering from wounds,
A Bhojājānīya Sindh horse is still superior to a common horse. Therefore, harness me alone to the chariot.

## Gojānīya Jātaka, the Third.

## 24. Ājañña Jātaka

Whenever, in whatever place, at whatever moment,
On whatever battlefields, and at whatever time,
A noble steed (Ājāniya) puts forth effort, at that time of effort, the common horses fall behind.

## Ājañña Jātaka, the Fourth.
7:
## 25. Tittha Jātaka

Charioteer, let the auspicious horse drink and bathe at various different watering places.
A man who has become fat from overeating becomes satiated even with milk-rice.

## Tittha Jātaka, the Fifth.

## 26. Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka
The elephant Mahiḷāmukha, having heard the words of former thieves, followed their example and went about striking others.
The noble elephant Mahiḷāmukha, having truly heard the words of monks and brahmins who are well-restrained in body, speech, and mind, has now become established in all virtues.

## Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka, the Sixth.

## 27. Abhiṇha Jātaka
He is unable to eat the first morsel of rice offered, nor the ball of rice, nor the grass; nor is he able to rub his body.
I think the state elephant has formed a friendship with the dog through constant seeing.

## Abhiṇha Jātaka, the Seventh.

## 28. Nandivisāla Jātaka
One should speak only pleasant words; one should never speak unpleasant words.
For the one who spoke pleasant words, the bull pulled the heavy load.
He also caused that brahmin to obtain wealth; therefore, that brahmin became delighted in mind.

## Nandivisāla Jātaka, the Eighth.

## 29. Kaṇha Jātaka
Wherever the load is heavy, and wherever the path is deep and difficult,
At that time, they harness Kaṇha (the black bull), and that bull carries that heavy load.

## Kaṇha Jātaka, the Ninth.
8:
## 30. Munika Jātaka
Do not envy Munika for the food he receives; Munika eats the rice of death.
Being free from anxiety, eat plenty of your own food; eating in this way is the sign of long life.

## Munika Jātaka, the Tenth.

## Kuruṅgavagga, the Third.
The summary of that chapter is:
Kuruṅga Jātaka, Kukkura Jātaka, the noble Bhojājānīya Jātaka, then Ājañña Jātaka, Tittha Jātaka,
The pleasant Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka, Mudupāṇi Jātaka, Kaṇha Jātaka who carries the load, and Munika Jātaka—these are the ten.

## 4. Kulāvakavagga

## 31. Kulāvaka Jātaka
O Mātali, there are nests of young Garuḍas in this silk-cotton tree; avoid it with the chariot pole.
Let us rather lose our lives to the Asuras, but let not the nests of these young birds be destroyed.

## Kulāvaka Jātaka, the First.

## 32. Nacca Jātaka
Your cry is pleasant, your back is beautiful, and your neck has a hue like that of lapis lazuli.
Your wings are a fathom in length, yet because of your dancing (and lack of shame), I will not give you my daughter.

## Nacca Jātaka, the Second.
9:
## 33. Sammodamāna Jātaka
The birds fly away taking the net while they are in harmony and rejoicing together. When those birds fall into dispute, then they will come under my power.

## Sammodamāna Jātaka, the Third is finished.

## 34. Maccha Jātaka
Neither cold nor heat nor the entanglement in the net distresses me. But that the female fish should think, "This fish has gone to another female for pleasure," that thought alone truly distresses me.

Maccha Jātaka, the Fourth is finished.

## 35. Vaṭṭaka Jātaka
I have wings, but they cannot yet fly. I have feet, but they cannot yet walk. My parents have left me and gone. O Fire, go back and depart!

## Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, the Fifth is finished.

## 36. Sakuṇa Jātaka
The birds depend on this tree, yet this very tree is emitting fire. O assembly of birds, flee to the various directions; danger has arisen from our very refuge.

## Sakuṇa Jātaka, the Sixth is finished.

## 37. Tittira Jātaka
Those men who respect the elders and are skilled in the Dhamma are praiseworthy in this very life and reach a happy destination in the next life.

## Tittira Jātaka, the Seventh is finished.

## 38. Baka Jātaka
A person of treacherous wisdom does not attain excessive happiness through treachery. The person of treacherous wisdom only destroys himself, just as the crane was killed by the crab.

## Baka Jātaka, the Eighth is finished.
10:
## 39. Nanda Jātaka
I think there is a heap of gold and a golden wreath in that place where Nanda, the house-born slave, stands and shouts harsh words.

## Nanda Jātaka, the Ninth.

## 40. Khadirangāra Jātaka
Lord, let me truly fall headfirst into the hell that is the pit of glowing embers. I will not, however, perform the ignoble act of refusing to give alms. Please, Venerable Sirs, accept this alms-food.

## Khadirangāra Jātaka, the Tenth.

## Kulāvakavagga, the Fourth.
The summary of that chapter is:
Siri, Mātali, Dhītara, Pakkhivara, Ratiyāgata, Mātāpitā, Jagatīruha, Vuḍḍha, Sukakkuṭaka, and likewise Nandaka and the noble Piṇḍa—these are the ten Jātakas.

## 5. Atthakāmavagga

## 41. Losaka Jātaka
He who, though being advised by one who desires his welfare and is compassionate, does not follow the instruction, will grieve like Mittaka who seized the leg of the she-goat.

## Losaka Jātaka, the First.
11:
## 42. Kapota Jātaka
Whoever, being advised by one who desires his welfare and is compassionate, does not follow the instruction, like one who did not follow the words of the pigeon, lies fallen into the hands of the enemy (in death).

## Kapota Jātaka, the Second.

## 43. Veḷuka Jātaka
Whoever, being advised by one who desires his welfare and is compassionate, does not follow the instruction, meets with destruction and lies (dead), just as the father of the snake named Veḷuka lay dead (bitten by the snake).

## Veḷuka Jātaka, the Third.

## 44. Makasa Jātaka
A wise enemy is better; a friend devoid of wisdom is not noble at all. The foolish son, thinking "I will kill the mosquito," split his father's head.

## Makasa Jātaka, the Fourth.

## 45. Rohiṇī Jātaka
A wise enemy is better; a foolish friend who constantly looks after one is not noble at all. Look at the wretched Rohiṇī, who lacks discretion; having killed her mother, she is now grieving.

## Rohiṇī Jātaka, the Fifth.

## 46. Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka
For one unskilled in what is beneficial, the practice of benefit does not bring happiness. A person of little wisdom ruins the benefit, like the monkey in the garden.

## Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka, the Sixth.
12:
## 47. Vāruᅀidũsaka Jātaka
One who is unskilled in welfare is unable to bring about happiness by practicing for welfare. A person of little wisdom causes welfare to decline, just as Koᅀᅀa  a ruined the liquor.
## Vāruᅀidũsaka Jātaka, the seventh.
## 48. Vedabbha Jātaka
Whoever desires welfare through improper means meets with distress. The thieves of the Ceta country killed the Brahmin Vedabbha; all of them also met with destruction.
## Vedabbha Jātaka, the eighth.
## 49. Nakkhatta Jātaka
Benefit has passed by the fool who waits for a lucky star. Benefit itself is the star of benefit; what can the stars in the sky accomplish?
## Nakkhatta Jātaka, the ninth.
## 50. Dummedha Jātaka
I have prayed to offer a sacrifice with a thousand fools. Now I shall sacrifice; many people are unrighteous.
## Dummedha Jātaka, the tenth.

## 6. Āsīsa Vagga

## 51. Mahāsīlava Jātaka
A good man should indeed cherish hope (thinking, "I shall be free from this suffering"); the wise man should not despair. I see myself now just as I had desired.

## Mahāsīlava Jātaka, the First.

## 52. Cūḷajanaka Jātaka
A good man should indeed strive (thinking, "I shall be free from this suffering"); the wise man should not despair. I see myself now, having been brought from the water to the dry land.

## Cūḷajanaka Jātaka, the Second.

## 53. Puṇṇapāti Jātaka
The cups are full just as before, yet this talk (praising the liquor) is of a different sort and is untrue. By the appearance and the nature of the circumstances, I know this liquor is not good.

## Puṇṇapāti Jātaka, the Third.

## 54. Kiṃphala Jātaka
This tree is not difficult to climb, nor is it far from the village. By this very unusual circumstance, I know this tree does not have sweet fruit.

## Kiṃphala Jātaka, the Fourth.

## 55. Pañcāvudha Jātaka
The person who, with an undaunted heart and a mind free from shrinking, develops wholesome states for the sake of attaining Nibbāna (security from the four yokes), shall reach in due course the destruction of all fetters (Arahantship).

## Pañcāvudha Jātaka, the Fifth.
14:
## 56. Kañcanakkhandha Jātaka
The person who, with a mind serene and joyful through the calming of defilements, develops faultless wholesome states for the sake of attaining Nibbāna (security from the four yokes), reaches in due course the destruction of all fetters (Arahantship).

## Kañcanakkhandha Jātaka, the Sixth.

## 57. Vānarinda Jātaka
O King of Monkeys, he who possesses these four qualities as you do—Truth, Wisdom, Fortitude, and Liberality—overcomes the enemy he sees.

## Vānarinda Jātaka, the Seventh.

## 58. Tayodhamma Jātaka
O King of Monkeys, he who possesses these three qualities as you do—Skillful Effort, Courage, and Wisdom—overcomes the enemy he sees.

## Tayodhamma Jātaka, the Eighth.

## 59. Bherivādaka Jātaka
One should beat the drum, but not excessively; excessive beating indeed brings a bad result. By moderate beating, a hundred coins were gained; by excessive beating, that acquired wealth was lost.

## Bherivādaka Jātaka, the Ninth.

## 60. သင်္ခဓမဇာတကံ
One should blow the conch, but not excessively; excessive blowing indeed brings a bad result. The wealth acquired by moderate blowing was ruined by the father through excessive blowing.

## Saṅkhadhama Jātaka, the Tenth.

## Āsīsa Vagga, the Sixth.

The summary of this vagga is:
There are ten Jātakas marked by the words: Yathā, Icchiṃ, Tathā, Udakā, Thala, Sura, Sāduphala, Alīnamana, Sampahaṭṭhamana, Caturo, Tayo, Sataladdhaka, and Bhogadhana.

## 7. Itthivagga

## 61. Asātamantajātaka
In this world, women are known to be unvirtuous and wicked; there is no limit or boundary to their conduct.
They are excessively lustful for sensual pleasures and are extremely harsh in body, speech, and mind. Like an all-consuming fire, they consume everything.
Mother, I shall renounce these women and, cultivating the state of seclusion, I shall go forth as a monk.

## Asātamantajātaka, the First.

## 62. Aṇḍabhūtajātaka
The Brahmin played the lute with his face and head wrapped in cloth for the purpose of deception.
Even wives who have been raised from the time they were eggs in the womb can become unfaithful; what wise person would ever place trust in such women?

## Aṇḍabhūtajātaka, the Second.

## 63. Takkapaṇḍitajātaka
Women are prone to anger, ungrateful, slanderous, and divisive among friends.
Monk, practice the holy life; by so practicing, you shall live in happiness.

## Takkapaṇḍitajātaka, the Third.

## 64. Durājānajātaka
Do not be delighted thinking, "This woman desires me," nor be grieved thinking, "This woman does not desire me."
The nature of women is difficult to know, just like the path of a fish in water.

## Durājānajātaka, the Fourth.
16:
## 65. Anabhiratijātaka
Just as a river, a road, a tavern, a hall, and a water-stand are common to all people, so too in this world are women common to all. Therefore, the wise do not get angry with them.
## Anabhiratijātaka, the Fifth.

## 66. Mudulakkhaṇajātaka
Great King, before I obtained Queen Mudulakkhaṇā, I had only one desire to possess her. From the moment I obtained that beautiful-eyed queen, that desire multiplied and gave birth to other desires.
## Mudulakkhaṇajātaka, the Sixth.

## 67. Ucchaṅgajātaka
Great King, a son is easily obtained in one's lap, and a husband is easily found even while traveling on the road. But as for a brother born of the same womb, I no longer see that place—the mother's womb—from which I could bring him, for my parents have passed away.
## Ucchaṅgajātaka, the Seventh.

## 68. Sāketajātaka
Monks, even if it is a person never seen before in this life, if at the mere sight of them the heart is established in love and the mind is clear, one should certainly be intimate with that person because of past intimacy in previous lives.
## Sāketajātaka, the Eighth.

## 69. Visavantajātaka
Cursed be that poison which I, for the sake of living, would swallow again after vomiting it. To me, death is better than such a life.
## Visavantajātaka, the Ninth.

## 70. Kuddālajātaka
Great King, a victory that can be overturned by enemies is not a good victory. Only a victory that cannot be overturned by enemies is truly a good victory.
## Kuddālajātaka, the Tenth.

## Itthivagga, the Seventh.
17:
The summary verse of this vagga is:
Sikhī, Sabbaghasa, Vīṇavara, Pisuṇa, Mittabhedika, Nandīvisāla, Kaṇhanadī, Mudulakkhaṇa, Sodariya, Mano, Visaveyya, and Sādhusīla Jātakas are the ten.

## 8. Varuṇavagga

## 71. Varuṇajātaka
71. He who wishes to do later the tasks that should have been done first, will later regret it, like the youth who broke the green Varuna wood.

## Varuṇajātaka, the First.

## 72. Sīlavahatthijātaka
72. To an ungrateful man who is always looking for faults, even if one were to give the entire earth, one could not satisfy him.

## Sīlavahatthijātaka, the Second.

## 73. Saccāṃkirajātaka
73. In this world, some people have said this true word: "It is better to salvage a log floating in the water than to salvage some people."

## Saccāṃkirajātaka, the Third.

## 74. Rukkhadhammajātaka
74. Many relatives are excellent when they are united. Even trees growing in the forest are excellent if they stand together in great numbers. A lone giant tree, however, can be toppled by a strong wind.

## Rukkhadhammajātaka, the Fourth.
18:
## 75. Macchajātaka
O Pajjunna, King of Devas, thunder and rain! Destroy the fish's hiding place in the mud with a flood so that the crow cannot eat it. Make the crow suffer with grief, and release me from my sorrow.

## Macchajātaka, the Fifth.

## 76. Asaṅkiyajātaka
I have no apprehension in the village, nor do I have fear in the forest. I have ascended the straight path of the Divine Abodes through loving-kindness and compassion.

## Asaṅkiyajātaka, the Sixth.

## 77. Mahāsupinajātaka
Bulls, trees, cows and calves, horses, a golden bowl, a jackal and a water pot,

A pond, raw rice and sandalwood; gourds sink, and stones float.

Small frogs swallow cobras; golden geese surround a crow;

Panthers tremble with fear of goats. Perversion is occurring; in this time, there is no beneficial effect yet.

## Mahāsupinajātaka, the Seventh.

## 78. Illisajātaka
Both are lame, both have crooked hands, both are cross-eyed,

On both of them, lumps have appeared on their heads; I can no longer recognize this person as the Treasurer Illisa.

## Illisajātaka, the Eighth.
19:
## 79. Kharassara Jātaka
O friends, when the cattle are plundered and slaughtered, when the houses are burnt and the people are led away as slaves, then the son of the woman whose son was killed came playing a harsh-sounding drum.

## Kharassara Jātaka, the Ninth.

## 80. Bhīmasena Jātaka
Bhīmasena, in the past before the battle, you spoke words of self-praise while disparaging others. Now, on the battlefield, you are leaking foul excrement and urine. Bhīmasena, your talk of war and your current exhaustion from fear do not match.

## Bhīmasena Jātaka, the Tenth.

## Varuṇa Vagga, the Eighth.
The summary of that chapter is:
Varuṇa Jātaka, Akataññū Jātaka, Saccavara Jātaka, Savanappati Jātaka, Abhitthanaya Jātaka, Karuṇāya Jātaka, Silāplava Jātaka, Illisa Jātaka, Diṇḍima (Kharassara) Jātaka, and Pūtisara (Bhīmasena) Jātaka—thus there are ten.

## 9. Apāyimha Vagga

## 81. Surāpāna Jātaka
Teacher, we have drunk, we have danced, we have sung, and we have cried. Though we drank the intoxicant that causes loss of mindfulness and madness, we have not yet become like the monkeys seen before our eyes.

## Surāpāna Jātaka, the First.
20:
## 82. Mittavindaka Jātaka
Mittavindaka, you have passed the crystal palace, the silver palace, and the ruby palace, and now you sit on a stone slab where the razor-wheel has reached. As long as your demerit is not exhausted, you shall not be released from that razor-wheel while alive.

## Mittavindaka Jātaka, the Second.

## 83. Kālakanṇi Jātaka
By walking seven steps together, one becomes a friend. By living together for twelve days, one becomes a companion. By living together for a fortnight or a month, one becomes like a kinsman. Beyond that, one becomes like one's own self. How then can I, for the sake of my own happiness, abandon a friend named Kāḷakaṇṇi with whom I have associated for so long?

## Kālakanṇi Jātaka, the Third.

## 84. Atthassadvāra Jātaka
One should desire the supreme gain of health, virtue praised by the wise, learning, following the Dhamma, and tireless effort. These six qualities are the primary gates to welfare.

## Atthassadvāra Jātaka, the Fourth.

## 85. Kiṃpakka Jātaka
He who indulges in sensual pleasures without knowing the danger that will arise in the future is killed by them at the time of their fruition, like the poisonous Kiṃpakka fruit that has been eaten.

## Kiṃpakka Jātaka, the Fifth.

## 86. Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka

A noble person of virtuous conduct, who perceives the benefit through wisdom, should not associate with a person of evil conduct who is loathsome.
Just as the elephant committed an evil deed by killing the ascetic Indasamānagotta, even so, an evil person may commit an evil deed even after living together for a long time.

One should form a friendship only with one whom one knows to be equal to oneself in virtue, wisdom, and learning.
Indeed, association with a virtuous person brings happiness.

## First: Indasamānagotta Jātaka.

## 162. Santhava Jātaka (2-2-2)

There is no deed more evil than associating with an evil person.
Even though it was satisfied with ghee and milk-rice, this fire has burned down the leaf-hut that was built with great difficulty.

There is no deed more noble than associating with a virtuous person.
The golden-hued doe Sāmā, because of her loving friendship, licks the faces of the lion, the tiger, and the leopard.

## Second: Santhava Jātaka.

Mongoose, you have made friends with your enemy, the egg-born snake, and sleep with your fangs bared; from where does fear come to you? One should be suspicious of an enemy and should not trust even a friend. Fear arising from a friend thought to be safe cuts off even the very roots.

## 166. Upasāጰaka Jātaka (2-2-6)
In this place, fourteen thousand people named Upasāጰaka have been cremated; there is no place in the world that is not a cemetery. In whom there is truth, righteousness, non-violence, restraint, and self-control—the Noble Ones associate with such a person; that quality is called the deathless state (Nibbāna) in the world.
## Upasāጰaka Jātaka is the sixth.

## 167. Samiddhi Jātaka (2-2-7)

Bhikkhu, in your youth, you go about for alms without enjoying sensual objects through the power of defilements. Is it not proper to practice for alms only after enjoying the five kinds of sensual pleasures?
Bhikkhu, you go about for alms without enjoying sensual pleasures; do not let the time of youth pass you by.

O goddess, I do not know the time when I shall die; the time of death is not apparent, being shrouded by delusion.
Therefore, I go about for alms, thinking, "May the time not pass me by," without enjoying sensual pleasures.

## 168. Sakunagghi Jātaka (2-2-8)

Monks, when a falcon swooped down with force upon a quail who remained in his own territory in a ploughed field, the falcon reached his death because of that swift action.

I, being endowed with the wisdom that knows the means of escape from danger, and delighting in the territory that is the heritage of my parents, am free from the enemy and rejoice because I clearly see my own benefit.

## 169. Araka Jātaka (2-2-9)

O group of ascetics, whoever protects the entire world of beings with a mind of immeasurable loving-kindness in all ways—above, below, and across.

There is that (fine-material sphere) mind, full and well-developed, desiring the welfare of beings, taking immeasurable beings as its object. Whatever (sense-sphere) kamma is performed in a limited way, that kamma cannot remain by overwhelming that (fine-material sphere) meritorious kamma.

Great King, because this little chameleon has obtained a half-māsa coin, which he never obtained before, he even disregards the Great King, the Lord of the Videha country, who reigns over the great city of Mithilā.

Who makes Mount Daddara echo with such a great sound? Why do the lions not roar in response? What is the name of this creature, the lord of beasts?

Where have you ever heard or seen such a thing as a virtuous monkey? Now I will void excrement upon you; this is the very nature (dhamma) of us monkeys.

Among all beings, there are indeed those endowed with virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi). Look at this base monkey; he stands worshipping the sun.

You praise this monkey without knowing his conduct. This vile monkey has voided excrement in our fire-chamber and has also broken two water jars (kamaṇḍalu).

## 176. Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi Jātaka (2-3-6)
O King, lord of men, this monkey that roams the tree branches truly has no wisdom; having scattered a whole handful of peas, he searches for only the one pea that fell.

O King, just as the monkey searching for one pea loses all the peas because of that one, so we and others who are overly greedy will destroy great benefits for a small reason.

## 177. Tinduka Jātaka (2-3-7)
Men with bows and arrows in hand, carrying noble swords, have surrounded us on all sides; how shall we escape from the danger of death?

O monkeys, for those with many affairs, some other matter may arise; there are still unpicked fruits on the Tinduka tree; eat the Tinduka fruits as much as you desire.

"This is my birthplace, this is where I grew up"—clinging thus, I stayed in the mud; that mud has oppressed me, just as the strong oppress the weak. Bhaggava, listen to my words; I shall tell you.

Whether in a village or a forest, wherever one finds happiness, that is the birthplace and the place of growth for a person who understands the cause. One should go where one can live; do not be killed by being attached to a dwelling place.

Great King, ruler of men, that group of donkeys, being of low birth, is oppressed by intoxication because of their low nature, even after drinking a liquid of little flavor. Great King, if a horse-trainer with well-groomed hair and beard, suitable for that horse, were to take it by the reins and lead it around the stable, that horse would quickly abandon its limping and follow only the example of that man who walks gracefully.

## 185. Anabhirati Jātaka (2-4-5)
Just as when water is turbid and not clear, one cannot see shells, snails, gravel, sand, and shoals of fish; likewise, when the mind is turbid (with passion, etc.), one cannot see one's own benefit or the benefit of others.

Just as when water is clear and especially pure, one can see shells, snails, gravel, sand, and shoals of fish; likewise, when the mind is not turbid but clear, one can see one's own benefit and the benefit of others.

## 186. Dadhi vāhana Jātaka (2-4-6)
This mango tree was formerly endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor. While receiving the same offerings as before, why does this mango tree now bear bitter fruit?

O King Dadhivāhana, who possesses an army, your mango tree is surrounded by Pucimanda (neem) trees. The roots of the mango tree are entangled with the roots of the Pucimanda trees, and the branches of the mango tree lean upon and intertwine with the branches of the Pucimanda trees. Because of its association with the unpleasant Pucimanda trees, for that reason, the mango tree bears bitter fruit.

O young geese, you have climbed onto a high fork of a tree and are consulting in private. Descend to a lower place and consult; let the jackal, who is the king of beasts, also listen.

When a beautiful goose consults with another beautiful goose, and a god-like goose with another god-like goose, what benefit is there for you here, O jackal, who claims to be pure in the four attributes (body, lineage, voice, and virtue)? O jackal, enter your hole at once.

## Catumaṭṭha Jātaka, the Seventh.

## 216. Maccha Jātaka (2-7-6)

This fire does not burn me, nor does this well-sharpened spit hurt me. Only the thought that my female fish will think, 'This fish has gone to enjoy himself with another female,' burns me.

Only that fire of passion burns me and distresses my mind. O masters of the net, release me; one should not be killed anywhere because of sensual desire.

Maccha Jātaka, the sixth.

## 217. Seggu Jātaka (2-7-7)

Seggu, all the world rejoices as they please; you alone remain unskilled in the ways of the world. When caught in the forest, are you weeping because of your maidenly virtue?

The father himself, who should be a refuge when suffering comes, is committing a wrong in the forest. When the protector himself acts with violence, to whom shall I cry out in the middle of this forest?

## Seggu Jātaka, the seventh.

## 218. Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka (2-7-8)
This extreme deceit of a deceitful person is well-planned; it is a counter-deceit returned to a crooked person. If mice could eat an iron plowshare, why could hawks not carry away a child?

In this world, there are those who are crooked in return to a deceitful person; there are those who act with deceit against a deceitful person. O you who lost your son, give the plowshare to the one who lost his plowshare; let not the one who lost his plowshare take away your son.

## 219. Garahita Jātaka (2-7-9)
The talk of foolish people who do not see the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, both by night and by day, is always this: 'My silver, my gold.'

In a house, there are two householders each; of those two, one householder has no beard or whiskers, has long breasts, and has hair braided in various ways; moreover, has ears pierced for wearing earrings. That householder, bought with much wealth, stings that group of people with her mouth.

## Garahita Jātaka, the ninth.

Brahmin, you seem to live happily; having come from the inhabited country to this waterless great forest, why do you meditate alone at the foot of a tree like a destitute person?

Friend, I seem to live happily; having come from the inhabited country to this waterless great forest, living alone at the foot of a tree, I meditate, repeatedly recollecting the nature of the Dhamma of the virtuous.

This is the advice of the teacher, which the ancient teacher Pārāsariya once said: "Do not do evil which you will later regret."

## 227. Gūthapāṇa Jātaka (2-8-7)
A brave man, possessing great effort and capable in battle, has met another brave man. O great elephant, come back! Return! Why do you flee in fear? Let the people of Aṅga and Magadha witness my prowess and yours.

I shall not kill you with my feet, nor with my tusks, nor with my trunk. I shall kill you with dung alone; let the foul dung-beetle be slain by foul dung.

## Gūthapāṇa Jātaka, the seventh.

## 228. Kāmanīta Jātaka (2-8-8)
O Brahmin, I desire the kingdoms of Pañcāla, Kuru, and Kekaka, which lie within the three mountain-like cities. O Brahmin, I desire the three great kingdoms beyond those as well. O Brahmin, if you wish to cure me, who am oppressed by sensual desires, then cure me.

Some wise men provide a cure for one bitten by a cobra. Some wise men provide a cure for one possessed and oppressed by a spirit. No one but a wise man can cure one destroyed by sensual desires. For one who has transcended merit and stands in demerit, what kind of cure would be of benefit?

## Kāmanīta Jātaka, the eighth.

## 229. Palāyita Jātaka (2-8-9)
With noble elephants trumpeting like cranes and resembling rain clouds, with noble horsemen adorned with golden crests, with chariot-warriors as fierce as ocean waves, with archers who rain down arrows like a dense downpour, and with infantrymen who strike fiercely wielding swords, Takkasilā is surrounded on all sides.
63:
O soldiers, run forward and approach the city! The elephants are trumpeting various sounds. Today, a tumultuous noise is arising. Like the lightning of a thundering rain cloud, the soldiers are rushing forth.

## Palāyita Jātaka, the ninth, is finished.

## 230. Dutiya Palāyita Jātaka (2-8-10)
My banners are immeasurable and numerous. My army is as vast as the shoreless ocean. Just as crows are unable to overcome the ocean, enemies are unable to oppress or overcome this army.

Just as the wind cannot shake a great mountain, a person like you cannot overcome me today.

Do not lament foolishly; there will be no such benefit for you. Since there is no one to restrain you, you will meet with destruction.

It is as if you have offended a lone-wandering great elephant. That great elephant will trample and destroy you, just as one tramples a reed with his foot.

## 9. Upāhana Vagga

## 231. Upāhana Jātaka (2-9-1)
Just as shoes that are bought and worn for a man's comfort may, due to the heat of summer or the soreness of the soles, turn back and bite that man's own feet.

Even so, an unworthy person of low birth, having acquired knowledge and learning from a teacher, uses that very knowledge to oppress that teacher. Such a person is called an ignoble man, comparable to a biting shoe.

## Upāhana Jātaka, the first.

## 232. Vīṇāguṇa Jātaka (2-9-2)
You alone have planned this matter. This youth has no wisdom and is not a leader. O lady, you are not fit to consort with one who has a crooked back.

Thinking him to be a bull among men, I fell in love with that hunchback. Now he lies curled up like a lute with broken strings.

## Vīṇāguṇa Jātaka, the second.

## 233. Vikaṇṇa Jātaka (2-9-3)
O crocodile, go indeed to wherever you wish to go. You have been pierced in a vital spot by a barbless arrow. Greedy and pursuing fish, you have been killed by the food provided with pleasant music.
65:
In this way, one who enters into worldly lures and follows the will of the mind suffers. Such a person perishes in the midst of kinsmen and friends, like the crocodile that followed the fish.

## Vikaṇṇa Jātaka, the third.

## 234. Asitābhū Jātaka (2-9-4)
O prince, you yourself have now brought about this state for me; my sensual desire for you has departed. That desire for you will never be reconnected; it is like an elephant's tusk severed by a sword.

Through excessive longing for various objects and through the intoxication of extreme greed, one thus falls away from one's benefit, just as I have fallen away from Princess Asitābhū.

## Asitābhū Jātaka, the fourth.

## 235. Vacchanakha Jātaka (2-9-5)
Vacchanakha, houses provided with gold and food are pleasant. In such a house, one may sleep without anxiety after eating and drinking.

Houses cannot be maintained for one who does not strive, nor for one who does not speak lies, nor for one who does not inflict punishment (does not oppress others). Who would take charge of a house that is so full of flaws and difficult to manage?

Vacchanakha Jātaka, the fifth.

## 236. Baka Jātaka (2-9-6)
This bird is truly beautiful, a bird resembling a white lily. With its wings stilled, it appears to be meditating very gently.

You do not know the virtue of this crane; you praise it without knowing. This bird does not protect us; therefore, it remains motionless (watching for an opportunity).

## Baka Jātaka, the sixth.

## 237. Sāketa Jātaka (2-9-7)
"Blessed One, why is it that towards some individuals in this world, the heart becomes exceedingly peaceful and the mind becomes clear upon merely seeing them?"

## The Sāketa Jātaka is the seventh.

"Father, I pray you. Please speak a single word that encompasses many meanings and causes, by which we may achieve our goals."

"Dear son, know the single word: effort (vīriya) combined with wisdom and skill. When that effort is joined with virtue and perfected with patience, it is capable of bringing happiness to friends and suffering to enemies."

## The Ekapada Jātaka is the eighth.

## 239. Haritamaṇḍūka Jātaka (2-9-9)
"Friend Green Frog, do you enjoy seeing me, a venomous snake, entered into the mouth of a trap and being bitten by a school of fish?"

"(This wanderer) does not want what he sees, but wants only what he does not see. I think he will wander for a long time; he will not obtain what he desires. Friends, this Prince Pādañjali truly outshines everyone with his wisdom.

## 251. Saṅkapparāga Jātaka (3-1-1)

With an arrow washed with the water of passion, whetted on the whetstone of sensual thought, unadorned, excellent, and not made by fletchers;

Not drawn to the ear and shot, nor having feathers such as those of a peacock, but causing fever in all limbs—with that arrow of defilement, I have been pierced in the heart.

## 1. Saṅkapparāga Jātaka

## 252. Tilamuṭṭhi Jātaka (3-1-2)

Brahmin... even to this day, I still remember in my mind how you held me by the arm and beat me with a bamboo stick because of a handful of sesame.

Why have you come to me? Do you not delight in life? You once held me by the arm and beat me three times.

Indeed, a wise person of noble conduct restrains with punishment one who does wrong; the wise know that such restraint is merely instruction, not an act of enmity.

## 2. Tilamuṭṭhi Jātaka

## 253. Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka (3-1-3)

Because of this precious jewel, abundant and grand food and drink arise for me; because you are one who begs excessively, I cannot give that jewel to you, nor will I come to your hermitage again.
72:
O youth, just as a youth holding a stone-polished weapon in his hand threatens [to cut off the head], you make me terrified by begging for the jewel. I shall not give that jewel to you; you are an excessive beggar. I shall not come to your hermitage again.

One should not beg for the beloved possession of another. By begging excessively, one becomes hated. When the Naga king was asked for the jewel by the Brahmin, from then on, he went only to where he could not be seen.

## 254. Kuṇḍakakucchisindhava Jātaka (3-1-4)

[Young horse], you grew up eating coarse grass and eating rice-scum and bran. This used to be your food; why do you not eat it now?

Great noble merchant, in a place where they do not know [a noble man] by birth or by conduct, there I would eat even rice-scum and bran in abundance.

But you indeed know me as a noble horse of such nature. Knowing [my] power, I will not eat your bran, having come to you who know [my] power.

## 4. Kuṇḍakakucchisindhava Jātaka

## 255. Suka Jātaka (3-1-5)

As long as that bird knew moderation in food, it reached a long life and could support its mother.

But when that bird ate too much food, it then sank right there [in the ocean]. That bird was one who did not know moderation.

Therefore, knowing moderation in food is good; being without greed is also good. Those who do not know moderation sink; those who know moderation do not sink.

## 5. Suka Jātaka

## 256. Jarūdapāna Jātaka (3-1-6)
Merchants seeking water, while digging an old well, found iron, copper, tin, and lead. The merchants also found silver, gold, pearls, and many cat's-eye gems.

Not content with those treasures they had obtained, those merchants dug further and further, again and again. Then, the powerful dragon king with fierce poison who resided in that well killed those merchants with the power of his venom.

Therefore, one should dig only enough, and not dig excessively. Excessive digging is indeed evil. While wealth is obtained by digging enough, it is destroyed by excessive digging.

## Jarūdapāna Jātaka, the sixth.

## 257. Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka (3-1-7)
This wrinkle-faced monkey is frivolous and is not skilled in managing household affairs. He destroys whatever is done; such is the nature of this monkey breed.

This hair is not the hair of a wise one; this creature is not one who brings comfort to others. My father, King Janasandha, once taught me that this monkey knows nothing at all.

A person of such nature would not support his own mother, father, brother, or sister. My father, King Dasaratha, once taught me this.

## Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka, the seventh.

## 258. Mandhātu Jātaka (3-1-8)
As far as the moon and sun revolve and shine, illuminating the quarters, all living beings dwelling on the earth are but servants of King Mandhātu.

Even with a rain of coins, there is no satisfaction in sensual pleasures. Knowing that sensual pleasures provide little enjoyment and much suffering, the wise one—
74:
—that disciple of the Fully Enlightened One finds no delight even in heavenly pleasures. He delights only in the destruction of craving.

## Mandhātu Jātaka, the eighth.

## 259. Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka (3-1-9)

This ascetic has no accomplishment through science or art. He is not Your Majesty's kinsman, nor a childhood playmate. Why then does this ascetic Tirīṭavaccha, who carries a wooden tripod, receive the foremost alms?

To me, who was defeated in battle, alone, and suffering in a fierce, waterless forest, this ascetic performed a deed of rescue. He extended a hand of effort to me while I was oppressed by misery. Because of that extended hand, I was delivered from distress.

Only because of this ascetic Vaccha's act of rescue have I returned from the realm of Death to this world of the living. Dear son, this ascetic Tirīṭavaccha is worthy of honor and offerings. Give him requisites and offer sacrifices to him.

## Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka, the ninth.

## 260. Dūta Jātaka (3-1-10)

For the sake of the stomach, people come from afar even to beg from an enemy. I am a messenger of that stomach. O Lord of charioteers, do not be angry with me.

By day and by night, living beings follow the will of the stomach. I am a messenger of that stomach. O Lord of charioteers, do not be angry with me.
75:
Brahmin, I give you a thousand red cows along with a bull. For how can a messenger not give to another messenger? We too are but messengers of that same stomach; we must surely give—thus the King said.

## Dūta Jātaka, the tenth.

## 261. Paduma Jātaka (3-2-1)

Just as hair and beard, though cut again and again, grow back,
So may your nose grow back; being entreated, please give me a lotus.

Just as the seed stored in the autumn season grows when sown in the field,
So may your nose grow back; being entreated, please give me a lotus.

Both of these are lamenting falsely, desiring to obtain lotuses;
Whether your nose grows or not, a severed nose cannot grow back.
Friend, being entreated, give me the lotuses; I beg of you—thus he said.

## Paduma Jātaka, the first.

## 262. Mudupāṇi Jātaka (3-2-2)

If the hand were soft, and the elephant well-trained,
And if it were dark and raining, only then would your desire surely be fulfilled.
76:
Women are not fit to live with men. They have firm hearts but soft and pleasant speech. Like a river, they are difficult to satisfy. Knowing this, the wise one, realizing that they lead to sinking into hell, should avoid them from afar.

Whichever man they serve, whether through mutual desire or through the giving of wealth, they quickly consume that man, just as fire consumes its own place of dwelling.

This ascetic, having come by psychic power over the unmoving water, fell into a miserable state and sank into the great ocean after engaging in human conduct with a woman.

Women turn the mind with sensual pleasures; they have great deceit and destroy the holy life. Knowing this, the wise one, realizing that they lead to sinking into hell, should avoid them from afar.

Whichever man they serve, whether through mutual desire or through the giving of wealth, they quickly consume that man, just as fire consumes its own place of dwelling.

Bhaddaji, it was exactly as you say. At that time, I was the one who performed your great and small services.

Vātaggasindhava Jātaka (3-2-6) Mother, for what reason, because of your mind being attached to that Sindhu horse, do you have a thin and pale body? For what reason does food not bring you pleasure? Has that noble Sindhu horse not come? Why do you flee now? Son, if what is called intimacy occurs at the very beginning, the wealth and retinue of women decline; therefore, son, I flee. A woman who does not desire a man born of a noble family and endowed with wealth and retinue who has come to her, will grieve for a long time, just as the mare named Bhaddalī grieved because she did not get the Sindhu horse named Vātagga. ## The Vātaggasindhava Jātaka is the sixth.
78:
## 267. Kakkataka Jātaka (3-2-7)
This golden crab, which has a color like gold (or serves the purpose of a horn), has no rudder, has protruding long eyes, has skin like bone, lives in water, and is hairless—having been caught and oppressed by its pinchers, I cry out piteously. Do not abandon me, who is as dear as life.

Lord, I will not abandon you, the noble elephant who is not less than sixty years of age. In this earth bounded by the four oceans, you are most dear to me.

Among the crabs in the ocean, the Gaṅgā, and the Yamunā, you, the water-born one, are the greatest in perfection of color and size of body. Because you are such a noble being, please release my husband who is crying.

## Kakkataka Jātaka, the seventh.

## 268. Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka (3-2-8)
If even the wisdom of a creature considered the best among all species is like this, what would the wisdom of other creatures besides that one be like?

O noble one, you blame us like this without knowing. Without seeing the roots, by what means can one know whether the roots of a standing tree are long or short?

I do not blame you, nor the other monkeys in the forest. In this matter, only King Vissasena, who obtained a person of your nature as a gardener to plant trees, should be blamed.

## Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka, the eighth.

## 269. Sujāta Jātaka (3-2-9)
Even if endowed with beauty, a pleasant voice, and a lovely appearance, a woman with harsh speech is not loved in this world or the next.

Mother, do you not see this cuckoo? Though black, unattractive, and spotted, it is loved by many beings because of its gentle voice.
79: Therefore, one who has gentle and polite speech, who speaks with judgment and wisdom, and who is firm without distraction of mind, shows the benefit and the cause. The speech of such a person is as sweet as honey. ## The Sujāta Jātaka is the ninth. ## 270. Ulūka Jātaka (3-2-10) I have heard that all the kinsmen have made the owl their chief. If the kinsmen permit, I wish to say a single word. Friend, permission is granted; speak only of the benefit and the cause completely. For there are birds who, though small in body, are wise and possess brilliant intellectual quality. O kinsmen, may you be free from danger and may good fortune be unto you. I do not like the consecration of the owl to be king. Look at the face of this owl who is not yet angry. If he should become angry, what kind of appearance will his face have? ## The Ulūka Jātaka is the tenth. ## Paduma Vagga is the second. The summary of that Vagga is: Paduma Jātaka, Nāgasiri (Nayana) Jātaka, Samuddara (Mahaṇṇava) Jātaka, Yūpa Jātaka, the noble Khurappa Jātaka, then Bhaddali Jātaka, Kuñjara Jātaka, Rukkha Jātaka, Kharavāca Jātaka, and the noble Ulūka Jātaka; thus ten are complete. ## 3. Udapāna Vagga ## 271. Udapānadūsaka Jātaka (3-3-1) Friend, why do you foul this well, which was laboriously made by forest-dwelling hermits who have practiced austerities for a long time, by voiding excrement and urine? O hermit, it is the nature of jackals that we void excrement and urine after drinking water. It is a custom descended from our fathers and grandfathers. You should not find fault with that nature.
80:
If this conduct of yours is such, then what would unrighteousness be like? We do not wish to see your conduct or your misconduct even for a moment.

## The Udapānadūsaka Jātaka is the first.

## 272. Byaggha Jātaka (3-3-2)

Through association with which friend one's well-being declines, a wise person should recognize the destruction caused by that wicked friend beforehand, just as one sees a spot on a tree.

Through association with which friend one's well-being increases, a wise person should treat that friend as himself in all matters and associate with him.

O lions and tigers, return from this place; go back to the great forest. Let not people cut down the forest that is without lions and tigers, and let not the lions and tigers reach a place without a forest.

## The Byaggha Jātaka is the second.

## 273. Kacchapa Jātaka (3-3-3)

Who is this person carrying [something] like a Brahmin with a full hand of offered alms? Where did he go for alms, and which faithful person did he approach?

I am a foolish monkey among monkeys; I have touched what should not be touched. Venerable sir, please release me; once free, I shall go to the mountain.

Tortoises are of the Kassapa lineage; monkeys are of the Koṇḍañña lineage. Release the Koṇḍañña monkey, O Kassapa; a sexual act has been committed by you.

## The Kacchapa Jātaka is the third.

## 274. Lola Jātaka (3-3-4)

Who is this female crane with a crest, who steals the place of a friend crow, and has a grandfather who leaps? O female crane, come this way; my friend crow is very fierce.

I am not a crested female crane; I am a greedy crow. Look at me, who has come here with feathers plucked because I did not follow your words.
81:
Friend crow, you will fall into such misery again. Your character is such that it leads to such suffering. Human pleasures are not things that can be easily enjoyed by birds.

## The Lola Jātaka is the fourth.

## 275. Rucira Jātaka (3-3-5)
This beautiful-bodied female crane stays in a crow's nest.
That crow, who is my friend, is fierce; this nest belongs to that crow.

O friend bird who eats millet, do you not know me?
Because I did not follow your advice, I have returned after having my feathers plucked.

Friend crow, you will fall into such misery again.
Your character is such that it leads to such suffering.
Human pleasures are not things that can be easily enjoyed by birds.

## The Rucira Jātaka is the fifth.

## 276. Kurudhamma Jātaka (3-3-6)
O Lord of the people, having known your faith and virtue,
we wish to exchange for the royal elephant, which has the color of black collyrium, to take to the Kaliṅga country.

In this world, whether it be one who is supported or one who is not, if they come with the intention of receiving alms,
the teaching of former teachers is that all such persons should not be refused.

O Brahmins, I give you this royal elephant, worthy of a king, a royal possession, of great renown,
adorned and covered with a golden net, along with its mahout.
Go wherever you desire.

## The Kurudhamma Jātaka is the sixth.
82: ## 277. Romaka Jātaka (3-3-7) O Romaka ascetic, born of a tree and having the color of a pigeon, we have lived in this mountain cave for over fifty years. In the past, those birds, without ceasing for even a day and without fearing danger, having very peaceful minds, would come to the place where I stretched out my hand. O ascetic with a crooked body, for what reason do those birds now see a contrary nature and fly away to another mountain cleft? Do they not regard me with respect as before? Or have these birds lived in another place for a long time and thus do not know me to be that same ascetic? Or are these birds not the old pigeons familiar to us, but other visiting birds? We know you; we are not very foolish or deluded. You are indeed that same ascetic whom we attended in the past; we are indeed those same pigeons who attended you in the past; we are not others. However, your mind has become malicious, wishing to harm and oppress this flock of pigeons. Therefore, we are afraid of you. ## The Romaka Jātaka is the seventh. ## 278. Mahiṃsarāja Jātaka (3-3-8) O King of Buffaloes, for what benefit do you endure the suffering of oppression from this monkey, who is light-minded and treacherous to friends, as if he were a master who grants all desires? Strike and crush this monkey with your horns, and trample him to pieces with your feet. If there is no one to forbid it, those of little wisdom will oppress you again and again. This monkey, thinking of me in this way, will do the same to other buffaloes. Then those fierce buffaloes will kill him; by their killing him, I shall be liberated from suffering and from the evil of taking life. ## The Mahiṃsarāja Jātaka is the eighth.

## 279. Satapatta Jātaka (3-3-9)
Just as a youth on the road mistakes a forest-dwelling jackal, who speaks desiring his welfare, for one who does not; and mistakes a woodpecker (Satapatta), who desires his harm, for one who desires his welfare.

In this same way, a certain person in this world is of such a nature. Even when spoken to with words concerning his welfare, he accepts them wrongly (in reverse).

Those who praise him, or flatter him out of fear—he regards them as his friends, just as the youth regarded the woodpecker as his friend.

## The Ninth, Satapatta Jātaka.

## 280. Puṭadūsaka Jātaka (3-3-10)
Indeed, this monkey-king seems to be skilled in the art of making leaf-packets. That is why he destroys the packet; surely he will make another.

Neither my mother nor my father was skilled in the art of making leaf-packets. We only destroy what has been made; such is the nature of our clan.

If such is your righteousness (dhamma), then what is unrighteousness like? May we never, at any time, see either your righteousness or your unrighteousness.

## The Tenth, Puṭadūsaka Jātaka.

## 4. Abbhantara Vagga

## 281. Abbhantara Jātaka (3-4-1)
There is a tree named Abbhantara, whose fruit is divine and fit for the gods. A woman with a pregnancy craving who eats this fruit gives birth to a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).

O Queen, you are the chief consort and beloved by your husband, the King. The King will bring this Abbhantara mango fruit for you.

A brave man who strives unremittingly for his master's sake, who is selfless and sacrifices his own life, attains a high position (of wealth and retinue). May I also be one who attains such a position.

## The First, Abbhantara Jātaka.

## 282. Seyya Jātaka (3-4-2)
He who associates with the superior (or with the superior Dhamma) becomes especially praiseworthy, better than he was before. By making peace with that single bandit chief, I saved seven hundred (ministers) from the danger of execution.

Therefore, by making peace with all people collectively, one should reach heaven in the life hereafter. O people of Kāsi, listen to these words.

The great King named Kaṃsa, who ruled over the city of Bārāṇasī, having spoken these words, cast away his bow and arrows, and entered into the practice of virtue as an ascetic.

## The Second, Seyya Jātaka.

## 283. Vaḍḍhakisūkara Jātaka (3-4-3)
O King of Tigers, formerly you roamed this place, oppressing the boars and killing the best of them. But now, why do you stand alone and hesitate? Has your strength vanished today?
85:
These boars used to flee in all directions in fear, seeking shelter. Now they dwell together in unity; because they stand thus united, even I find it difficult to overcome them.

Homage to the boars who have assembled in unity. Having seen for myself the wonderful friendship of the boars, I say this: The tusked boars, through the power of unity, have conquered even the tusked tiger and are liberated from the danger of death.

## The Third, Vaḍḍhakisūkara Jātaka.

## 284. Siri Jātaka (3-4-4)
Those without merit (luck) strive and accumulate much wealth. Whether skilled or unskilled, only the one with merit enjoys that wealth.

In every place, for the meritorious one who has performed good deeds, great wealth arises, surpassing other beings. It arises even in places where it is not easy for wealth to arise.

For the person who is without evil and has performed good deeds, roosters, gems, staffs, and women of virtuous marks come into being.

## The Fourth, Siri Jātaka.

## 285. Maṇisūkara Jātaka (3-4-5)
We have lived together, about thirty of us, in this crystal cave for seven years. We consulted together to destroy the luster of the gem.

However much we rub the gem, the gem only becomes more brilliant. Now we ask about this matter; what do you think of this affair?

This gem is a Veluriya (beryl) gem; it is flawless, pure, and beautiful. It is not possible to destroy the splendor of this gem. O boars, depart from this place.

## The Fifth, Maṇisūkara Jātaka.
86:
## 286. Sālūka Jātaka (3-4-6)
Do not long for the pig Sālūka's food; that pig eats the food of one who is about to die. You, being free from anxiety, eat only the bran; eating bran in this way is indeed the sign of long life.

Now, the bridegroom, along with his retinue, will come to this house as a guest. Then, you will see the pig Sālūka, with an upper lip like a pestle, lying dead and stiff.

Seeing the pig Sālūka dead, being cut into pieces while wailing, with an upper lip like a pestle, the two old oxen thought, "Only the bran, which is our food, is safe and noble."

## Sālūka Jātaka, the Sixth.

## 287. Lābhagaraha Jātaka (3-4-7)
One who does not act like a madman, does not slander, does not dance like an actor, and does not speak incoherently cannot obtain gain; only by acting thus among the foolish and deluded can one obtain gain. This is the advice given to you.

O Brahmin, despicable is the livelihood obtained by destroying oneself or by practicing unrighteousness, and despicable are the fame and wealth gained through such a livelihood.

Even wandering as a homeless monk, holding an alms-bowl to make a living, is noble. Such a livelihood is far superior and more noble than seeking a living through unrighteous practice.

## Lābhagaraha Jātaka, the Seventh.

## 288. Macchuddāna Jātaka (3-4-8)
These fish are worth more than a thousand coins; no one would believe this. I also have seven hundred coins here; I shall buy that lot of fish.

You fed the fish with rice and shared the merit with me. Remembering that merit you shared, I have performed this act of honor for you.
87:
That person who habitually does evil and deceives his brother because he does not wish to give the inheritance that is his father's property—to such a person with a corrupted mind, prosperity does not come, and the deities do not honor or protect him.

## The eighth, Macchuddāna Jātaka.

## 289. Nānāchanda Jātaka (3-4-9)

Great King, although we live together in one house, our desires are not the same. I desire a noble village; the Brahmin woman desires a hundred cows.

The son desires a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses; the daughter-in-law desires ruby earrings. This lowliest maidservant named Puṇṇikā desires a mortar and pestle.

Give the noble village to the Brahmin and the hundred cows to the Brahmin woman. Give the chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses to the son and the ruby earrings to the daughter-in-law. Also, give the desired mortar and pestle to this lowliest Puṇṇikā.

## The ninth, Nānāchanda Jātaka.

## 290. Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka (3-4-10)

The wise say that in this world, virtue alone is beautiful and good; virtue alone is supremely noble. Just as a snake with fierce venom is not harmed because it is "virtuous."

I will undertake that virtue which is accepted by the wise and which brings peace from danger. Because of being endowed with such virtue, a virtuous person is said to practice the conduct of the Noble Ones.

A virtuous person is loved by relatives and shines brightly among friends. When the body breaks up after death, the virtuous person reaches a good destination.

## The tenth, Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka.

## The fourth, Abbhantara Vagga, is finished.

The summary of that Vagga: Dumamedha Jātaka, Kaṃsavara Jātaka, Vyaggha Jātaka, Migālopa Jātaka, Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka, Maṇisūkara Jātaka, Sālūka Jātaka, Anusāsaniya Jātaka, Maccha Jātaka, and Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka.

## 5. Kumbha Vaggo

## 291. Surāghaṭa Jātaka (3-5-1)

A drunkard obtained a pot that could provide all desired objects, and as long as he could protect that pot from breaking, he enjoyed happiness.

When that drunkard became intoxicated and arrogant, he broke the pot through negligence. Then that fool became naked and had to wear rags, suffering thereafter.

In the same way, a foolish person who obtains wealth and consumes it negligently suffers later, like the drunkard who broke the pot.

## The first, Surāghaṭa Jātaka.

## 292. Supatta Jātaka (3-5-2)

Great King, in the city of Benares, there lived a Crow King named Supatta, surrounded by eighty thousand crows.

His wife, named Suphassā, had a pregnancy craving to eat the expensive royal food cooked in the King's kitchen.

I am a messenger sent by that Crow King and have come to this place before the King. Wishing to honor my master, the Crow King, I caused a wound on the nose (of the food-bearer).

## The second, Supatta Jātaka.
89:
## 293. Kāyanibbinda Jātaka (3-5-3)
Among the ninety-eight diseases, when one severe and violent disease strikes and oppresses me, bringing me to unbearable suffering, this body of mine withers away quickly, like a delicate flower cast upon the dust in the heat of the sun.

One who does not see the noble form (essence) in this body—which is regarded as noble (janya), designated as pure, yet is filled with various impurities—is thus affected.

Woe to this ailing, putrid body, loathsome, impure, and subject to disease! Beings who are negligent and deeply attached to this body lose the path to rebirth in the heavenly realms.

## The third, Kāyanibbinda Jātaka, is finished.

## 294. Jambukhādaka Jātaka (3-5-4)
Who is this bird, staying unsteadily on the rose-apple branch, crying with a sweet voice like a young peacock, possessing a rounded voice, a pleasant voice, and being supreme among those with voice?

A man of noble birth knows how to praise another man of noble birth with appropriate virtues. Friend jackal, who has a body like a young tiger, I give these rose-apples to you; eat them.

Indeed, after a long time, I see a liar met with another; the crow who eats the vomit of others and the jackal who eats carcasses, praising each other with false virtues and speaking untruths.

## The fourth, Jambukhādaka Jātaka, is finished.

## 295. Anta Jātaka (3-5-5)
King of beasts, your shoulders are like those of a bull. Your majestic bearing is like that of a lion. May there be salutation to the king of beasts! May we receive some food?

A man of noble birth knows how to praise another man of noble birth with appropriate virtues. Friend crow, whose color is like a peacock's neck, come down from this castor oil plant.
90:
Among beasts, the jackal is the lowest; among birds, the crow is the lowest. Among trees, the castor oil plant is the lowest. These three lowest ones have met here.

## The fifth, Anta Jātaka, is finished.

## 296. Samudda Jātaka (3-5-6)
Who is this bird that runs all around the salty ocean, forbidding the fish and sea-monsters (makaras), and becoming exhausted among the waves?

I am the bird known in all directions as Anantapāyī, the one who drinks the infinite ocean and is never satisfied. I wish to drink the entire Sāgara ocean, the lord of rivers.

That great ocean both ebbs and flows. Even though I drink, the limit of what is drunk is not apparent. Indeed, the Sāgara ocean cannot be exhausted by one drinker alone.

## The sixth, Samudda Jātaka, is finished.

## 297. Kāmavilāpa Jātaka (3-5-7)
O bird, who has wings as a vehicle and travels in the sky, flying in the high heavens, please tell my wife with smooth thighs that it has been a long time since I have come, and she will be longing for me.

She does not know of this sword set up, this impaling stake that is like a downward-facing blade. That fierce wife will be angry at my delay. It is only that anger that worries me; this stake does not worry me.

I have left ornaments like lotuses, gold rings, and soft Benares cloth at the head of the bed. May my dear wife, who desires wealth, take all those and be satisfied.

## The seventh, Kāmavilāpa Jātaka, is finished.

## 298. Udumbara Jātaka (3-5-8)
These cluster figs, banyan fruits, and wood-apple fruits are ripe. Come, come out and eat. Why do you wish to die of hunger?
91:
One who respects the elders becomes satisfied like this. I am satisfied today by eating ripe fruits such as the cluster fig.

The deception that a forest-born monkey would practice on another forest-born monkey might be believed by a young monkey like you, but an old, aged monkey like me would never believe it.

## The eighth, Udumbara Jātaka, is finished.

## 299. Komāruputta Jātaka (3-5-9)
O monkey, formerly you used to leap and play like a deer in the hermitage near the virtuous ascetics. O monkey, perform your monkey-like antics; we virtuous ascetics do not delight in your play.

I have heard the supreme and pure instruction of the highly learned ascetic Komāruputta. Friend, do not regard me as before; I now live devoted to the practice of meditative absorption (jhāna).

Just as if one were to sow seeds on a flat rock, even if it rains, those seeds would not grow; O monkey, you have merely heard that supreme and pure practice, but you are very far from the realm of jhāna.

## The ninth, Komāruputta Jātaka, is finished.

## 300. Vaka Jātaka (3-5-10)
Living by obstructing the lives of other beings and feeding on flesh and blood, a wolf undertook a vow and entered upon the fast (uposatha).

Sakka, knowing the wolf's vow, approached in the form of a goat. That wolf, who drinks the blood of beings, lost his fast and ran forward, breaking his own vow.
92:
In the same way, some in this Dispensation (Sāsana) are weak in the practice they have undertaken; because of a goat, they make themselves a laughing stock like the wolf.

## The tenth, Vaka Jātaka, is finished.

## The fifth, Kumbha Vagga.

Summary of the Jātakas:
The noble Kumbha, Supatta, Sirivhayana, Sucisammata, Bindusara, Usabha, Saritampati, Caṇḍi, Jarākapī, Makkaṭa, and Vaka Jātakas make ten (plus one).

Summary of the Vaggas:
The Tika Nipāta is adorned with the Saṅkappa Vagga, Paduma Vagga, the third Udapāna Vagga, Abbhantara Vagga, and Ghaṭabheda Vagga.

## The Tika Nipāta is finished.
