## 4. Catukkanipāta
## 1. Kāliṅgavagga
## 301. Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka (4-1-1)
O gatekeepers, commanded by the minister Nandisena, who is like a lion and well-trained by teachers, open this gate so that these princesses may enter the city of King Aruṇa.

Victory shall be to the Kaliṅga kings who possess hard-to-endure energy, and defeat and ruin shall be to the Assaka kings—thus said the ascetic practicing the noble life. The upright and virtuous do not speak falsehoods.

O Sakka, have the gods not transcended false speech? Among them, truth alone is the supreme wealth. O Maghavā, King of Gods, on what grounds did you speak such a falsehood?

O ascetic, have you not heard it said by others that the gods do not envy human effort? Self-control, unshakable concentration of mind, unity without discord, overcoming enemies and emerging victorious at the right time, firm persistence, and human effort—by these means alone did the victory of the Assakas come to be.

## Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka the First.

## 302. Mahāassāroha Jātaka (4-1-2)
One who gives to those unworthy of gifts and does not give to those worthy of gifts, when he encounters danger and suffering, he finds no good friend.
94:
One who does not give to those unworthy of gifts but gives to those worthy of gifts, when he encounters danger and suffering, he finds a good friend.

The recognition of the special benefits of association and shared enjoyment perishes among the ignoble and the deceitful. However, even a small favor done for the virtuous who are pure in conduct and upright yields great fruit.

He who has previously performed a noble favor and has done what is extremely difficult to do in the world—whether he performs a favor again later or not—is certainly worthy of constant honor.

## Mahāassāroha Jātaka the Second.

## 303. Ekarāja Jātaka (4-1-3)

O King Ekarāja, having formerly lived enjoying incomparable and noble sensual pleasures, why do you not now abandon your former complexion and strength, even though you have been cast into this uneven, hell-like pit?

O King Dabbasena, from long ago I have greatly yearned for patience (khanti) and ascetic practice (tapa). O Great King, now that I have attained those yearned-for qualities, why should I abandon my former complexion and strength?

For the famous, wise, and patient Great King, all duties have thus reached completion. Having attained a great fame (meditative absorption) never before achieved, he no longer abandons his former complexion and strength.

O King, ruler of men, whether discarding happiness for suffering or discarding suffering for happiness, I endure what is difficult for others to endure. The virtuous, being of an exceedingly peaceful nature in both happiness and suffering, remain equal in both states.

## Ekarāja Jātaka the Third.
95:
## 304. Daddara Jātaka (4-1-4)
Elder brother Daddara, these ill-spoken words in the human world cause me suffering. Those without venom revile me, who possess fierce venom, calling me a frog-eater and a water-snake living by the water's edge.

One who is banished from his own country and arrives in another land should build a great granary (of mindfulness and wisdom) to store away ill-spoken words.

In a place where a man is not known by his birth or by his conduct, one should not display pride while living among those who are not his kinsmen.

A wise man living in a foreign land should endure even the threats of a slave, just as one fears the danger of fire.

## Daddara Jātaka the Fourth.

## 305. Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka (4-1-5)
In this world, there is no such thing as a secret place for one who commits an evil deed. The forest deities see it; only the fool considers it a secret.

I do not see a secret place, nor does a place empty of beings exist. Even where I do not see another person, that place is not empty of me.

Dujjacca, Sujacca, Nanda, Sukhavaddhita, Vejja, and Addhuvasīla, though they desired a woman, had to abandon the possibility of obtaining her (due to their lack of virtue).

How could a Brahmin who has reached the further shore of all dhammas, who protects the Dhamma, and who is steadfast and possesses truthful effort, abandon the possibility of obtaining that woman?

## Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka the Fifth.
96:
## 306. Sujāta Jātaka (4-1-6)
O Great King, what are these fruits placed in the golden bowl—red in color, free from impurities, beautiful, and round? O Great King, being asked, please tell me about these fruits.

O Queen, in the past, with your hair disheveled and wearing tattered clothes, you used to gather jujube fruits with your hands into your lap. This fruit you are eating is the jujube fruit that comes from your own lineage.

This base woman, though living in the royal palace, is as if burning in hell; she cannot find delight. Fortunes abandon this luckless, base woman. Take this base woman back to that very place where she must live by gathering and selling jujube fruits.

O Great King, such faults of heedlessness often occur to women who have attained prosperity and retinue. O Great King, most excellent among chariot-warriors, please forgive Queen Sujātā; do not be angry with her.

## Sujāta Jātaka the Sixth.

## 307. Palāsa Jātaka (4-1-7)
O Brahmin, why do you, while knowing, persistently and heedfully ask this Palāsa tree—which is unconscious, cannot hear, and cannot know—about the benefit of sleeping soundly?

This Palāsa tree is famous even from afar; it is large and tall, situated on high ground, and is the abode of deities. Therefore, for the sake of wealth and prosperity, I pay homage to this Palāsa tree and to the powerful deities residing herein.

O Brahmin, seeing your gratitude, I shall favor you according to my power. Relying on the favor done in the presence of the virtuous, your efforts of body and speech shall not be in vain.
97:
O Brahmin, in front of the Tinduka tree stands a Pilakkha tree. Surrounding that Pilakkha tree is a great hidden treasure of gold that once had an owner. That treasure now has no heir. Go and dig up that treasure.

## Palāsa Jātaka, the seventh.

## 308. Sakuṇa Jātaka (4-1-8)

We have performed your task with all the strength we possessed. O King of Beasts, may there be homage to you. Shall we receive some meat?

For me, who constantly drinks blood and performs cruel deeds, that you are still alive while having entered between my teeth is a great favor you have received from me.

He who does not know a favor done, and does not return a favor, in such an ungrateful person there is no gratitude; associating with him is useless.

If from a person one cannot obtain the conduct of a friend despite a favor done in his presence, one should slowly depart from him without resentment or abuse.

## Sakuṇa Jātaka, the eighth.

## 309. Chavaka Jātaka (4-1-9)

All this that has been done is very lowly; both do not see the Dhamma. He who teaches the Vedas and he who learns the Vedas, both have fallen from their natural state.

I eat pure Sāli rice served with various meat curries. Because I am the master of that rice, I do not follow that Dhamma practiced by the sages (Isis).

O Brahmin, this world is vast; other beings also cook and eat. May that unrighteousness practiced by you not destroy you, as a stone breaks a pot.
98:
Brahmin... a way of life arises through evil that leads to the states of misery, or through unrighteous conduct. Such acquisition of fame, luxury, and wealth is truly contemptible.

## Chavaka Jātaka, the ninth.

## 310. Seyya Jātaka (4-1-10)

Even if one were to obtain this whole earth, encircled by the ocean as if the ocean were its earring, along with blame, one should not desire it. O Seyya... know this (my instruction) thus.

Brahmin... a way of life arises through evil that leads to the states of misery, or through unrighteous conduct. Such acquisition of fame, luxury, and wealth is truly contemptible.

Even if one were to wander as a homeless monk holding an alms bowl, that way of life (living on alms) is indeed more noble than seeking a livelihood through unrighteousness.

Even if one were to wander as a homeless monk holding an alms bowl, practicing without harming others in the world is more noble than even kingship.

## Seyya Jātaka, the tenth.

## Kālinga Vagga (Vivara Vagga), the first.

The summary of that Vagga is: Vivara Jātaka, Adeyya Jātaka, Samiddhavara Jātaka, Daddara Jātaka, Pāpa Jātaka, Mahā Jātaka, Tiraho Jātaka, Koli Jātaka, Palāsavara Jātaka, Kara Jātaka, and finally Sasamuddavara (Seyya) Jātaka—these are the ten.

## 2. Pucimanda Vagga

## 311. Pucimanda Jātaka (4-2-1)

Thief... arise! Why are you sleeping? What benefit is there for you in sleeping? May the king's men not capture you, who have committed a cruel theft in the village.
99:
Friend, deity of the Assattha tree, when the king's men capture the thief who committed a cruel theft in the village, what harm (danger) is there for the deity of the Nimb tree (Pucimanda) who stands in the forest?

Deity of the Assattha tree, you do not know the unsuitable connection between me and the thief. When the king's men capture the thief who committed a cruel theft in the village, they will impale him on a stake made of Nimb wood; for that reason, my mind is terrified.

A wise man should fear those dangers that ought to be feared; he should guard against future danger. Because the wise man fears future danger, he contemplates both this world and the next with wisdom.

## Pucimanda Jātaka, the first.

## 312. Kassapamandiya Jātaka (4-2-2)

Father of the Kassapa lineage, because of their lack of wisdom, youths might strike or abuse you. Even if they do so, a wise and prudent person should endure all those offenses committed by the youths; the wise should be patient with such faults.

If virtuous people quarrel, they quickly reconcile again. Fools, however, break like clay pots; they cannot reach a settlement of their enmity.

He who knows his own transgression and he who accepts the apology of another—these two, even if they have been divided, unite again; their reconciliation does not decay or perish.

He who, by himself, is worthy of reconciling others who have transgressed under the influence of anger, using pleasant words—such a person is called one who bears the burden of a great friend, one capable of carrying the load, more so than others.

## Kassapamandiya Jātaka, the second.

## 313. Khantivādī Jātaka (4-2-3)

O Great Heroic Ascetic, be angry only with that king who has cut off your hands, your feet, and your ears and nose; but do not let this country perish.

May that king who has cut off my hands, my feet, and my ears and nose live long; those like me do not get angry.

In times past, there was an ascetic who demonstrated the virtue of patience. The King of Kāsi caused the limbs, large and small, of that ascetic, who stood firm in patience alone, to be cut off.
100:
The result of that harsh evil deed was severe suffering; the King of Kāsi, falling into hell, experienced that result.

## The Khantivādī Jātaka is the third.

## 314. Lohakumbhi Jātaka (4-2-4)

We lived a bad life, for though we had wealth, we did not give; we did not make a refuge of merit for ourselves.

Sixty thousand years are now fully complete; when will there be an end for us who are being cooked in hell?

There is no end, where could there be an end? No end is seen; for then, friends, evil was done by both me and you.

If I go from this hell and obtain a human birth, I will be one who understands the requests of others, endowed with virtue, and I will perform many meritorious deeds.

## The Lohakumbhi Jātaka is the fourth.

## 315. Sabbamansalābha Jātaka (4-2-5)

Friend, though you are a beggar, your words are indeed harsh; because your words are like the membrane, I give you the membrane.

In this world, such a limb is called a brother; because your words are like a limb, I give you the flesh of my limb.

A son saying "Father" cools the father's heart; because your words are like the heart, I give you my heart.

If one has no friend in the village, that place is just like the forest; because your words are like everything, I give you all my flesh.

## The Sabbamansalābha Jātaka is the fifth.
101:
## 316. Sasapaṇḍita Jātaka (4-2-6)

(568) Brahmin, I have seven red fish that were brought from the water to the land by an otter. These fish are my property. Having roasted and cooked this fish-food which is my property, eat it and live in this forest, increasing your recluse-dharma at the foot of a pleasant tree as you please.

(569) Brahmin, in a place not far from my dwelling, the night meal of a field-watcher was certainly taken. There are two iguanas on a spit and a jar of curd; this much property I have. Having roasted and cooked all this and eaten as you wish, become one who observes the uposatha precepts and live in this forest, increasing your recluse-dharma at the foot of a pleasant tree.

(570) Brahmin, I have ripe mangoes of sweet flavor, cool water, and pleasant, cool shade. Having consumed all this property as you wish, live in this forest increasing your recluse-dharma.

(571) Brahmin, a rabbit has no sesame, no beans, and no rice. Eat my flesh cooked by this fire you have made, and live in this forest practicing the recluse-dharma.

## The Sasapaṇḍita Jātaka is the sixth.

## 317. Matarodana Jātaka (4-2-7)

(572) You weep only for those who have died. You do not weep for those who are yet to die. All beings who bear a body must give up their lives in turn when their time to die arrives.

(573) Devas, humans, four-footed animals, flocks of birds, and snakes endowed with wealth, having no mastery over their own bodies, give up their lives even while enjoying themselves without weariness in their place of birth.

(574) Repeatedly observing and reflecting with wisdom upon the pleasure and pain that are unstable and trembling among men, weeping and wailing is useless. Why do groups of sorrow overwhelm you?

(575) The debauched, the drunkards, the uneducated, the foolish, those who are bold in improper reflection, and those lacking good effort—being unskilled in the nature of worldly conditions—consider the wise man (who, knowing the worldly conditions according to reality, restrains himself with mindfulness and wisdom and does not weep at the death of kin) to be a "fool."

## The Matarodana Jātaka is the seventh.
103:
## 320. Succaja Jātaka (4-2-10)
O Father, the king who does not give even a mountain by word indeed cannot give up even an object that is easily relinquished. What benefit that I ask for could such a king possibly bestow?

A wise person should speak only of what they will do; they should not speak of what they will not do. The wise recognize a person who merely speaks but does not act as a liar.

O Prince, may there be salutation to you. You are established in the truth and in the nature of things. Even when you have fallen into distress, your mind delights only in the truth.

O Great King endowed with fame, that wife who suffers when her husband is poor and is happy when her husband is wealthy, following her husband's will, she alone is the supreme wife of that man. There are many women who wish to be the wife of a man rich in gold and silver.

## Succaja Jātaka, the tenth.
## Pucimanda Vagga, the second.
The summary of that chapter is: Cora Jātaka, Sakassapa Jātaka, Khantīvara Jātaka, Dujjīvita Jātaka, Vara Jātaka, Pharusa Jātaka, Sasa Jātaka, Mata Jātaka, Vasantasukha Jātaka, and Succaja Jātaka are the ten Jātakas included in this chapter.

## 3. Kuṭidūsaka Vagga
## 321. Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka (4-3-1)
O Monkey, your head is like a human's head, and your hands and feet are like a human's hands and feet. Yet, for what reason do you have no house?

O Singila bird, my head is like a human's head, and my hands and feet are like a human's hands and feet. However, that constructive wisdom, which is said to be the most excellent among humans, I do not possess.
104:
One who has an unstable mind, a fickle mind, who betrays friends, and who lacks constant virtue, cannot attain happiness.

O Monkey, exert the effort known as power for the arising of wisdom; transcend the habits of monkeys; build a nest that can protect you from the cold and the wind.

## Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka, the first.

## 322. Duddubha Jātaka (4-3-2)
Venerable Sir, in the place where I live, there is a "thud-thud" sound. I do not know what it is that makes such a "thud-thud" sound.

Hearing the sound of a falling bael fruit and saying "thud-thud (the earth is collapsing)," the hare fled. Hearing the words of the hare, the host of beasts fled in terror.

Fools who follow the voices of others without knowing the true cause, and who prioritize mere noise, tend to believe the words of others blindly.

Those wise ones who are endowed with virtue, who delight in the cessation of defilements (Nibbāna) through wisdom, and who keep far away from evil, are not those who believe the words of others without reason.

## Duddubha Jātaka, the second.

## 323. Brahmadatta Jātaka (4-3-3)
O King Brahmadatta, a beggar meets with two results: either not obtaining a gift or obtaining wealth; such is the nature of begging.

O Great King, the most excellent among the chariot-warriors of the Pañcāla kingdom, the wise call begging "weeping," and refusing a request they call "answering with weeping."

Let not the assembled people of the Pañcāla kingdom see me weeping or Your Majesty answering with weeping; therefore, I desire a secluded place.
105:
O Brahmin, who has abandoned evil, I give you a thousand red milch cows along with a bull. Having heard your verses endowed with Dhamma, why would one who is perfect in noble conduct not give to another who is perfect in noble conduct?

## Brahmadatta Jātaka is the third.

## 324. Cammasāṭaka Jātaka (4-3-4)
This noble ram with followers honors the Brahmin who is endowed with high birth and knowledge of the Vedas. This four-footed one indeed has a good nature, possesses great grace, and truly loves virtue.

O Brahmin, do not trust this four-footed ram just by seeing him for a moment. He retreats because he desires to strike hard; he will deliver a powerful blow.

The wanderer's thigh bone is broken, the bundle filled with requisites has rolled away, and all the wanderer's goods are destroyed. "The wanderer practicing the noble life is struck down! Run here!" he cries, raising both arms and weeping.

That person who praises one who is unworthy of honor lies struck down in this manner. It is just as I, of little wisdom, lie here today, having been struck down by the ram.

## Cammasāṭaka Jātaka is the fourth.

## 325. Godharāja Jātaka (4-3-5)
Thinking you were an ascetic, I approached you who are unrestrained. In the manner of one who is not an ascetic, you have struck me with a stick.
106:
O foolish ascetic, what is the use of your matted hair? What is the use of your antelope skin garment? Within you is a dense jungle of defilements, yet you polish only the exterior.

Come, King Lizard, return; eat this rice of the finest grain. I have oil and salt, and I have plenty of long pepper.

Wicked ascetic, you speak of having oil and salt. Having heard those words, I will retreat even further into this termite mound a hundred fathoms deep. Long pepper is of no use to me.

## Godharāja Jātaka, the fifth.

## 326. Kakkāru Jātaka (4-3-6)

He who does not take others' property with his body,
Who does not speak lies with his speech,
Who, though gaining fame and followers, does not become intoxicated—
He alone is worthy to wear the Kakkāru celestial flower.

One should seek wealth righteously,
One should not take wealth through deceit,
Who, though gaining riches, does not become intoxicated—
He alone is worthy to wear the Kakkāru celestial flower.

He whose mind is firm and does not fade quickly like turmeric dye,
Whose faith is also without decline,
Who does not enjoy delicious flavors alone—
He alone is worthy to wear the Kakkāru celestial flower.

Whether in one's presence or behind one's back,
He who does not disparage the virtuous,
And who acts as he speaks—
He alone is worthy to wear the Kakkāru celestial flower.

## Kakkāru Jātaka, the sixth.

## 327. Kākavatī Jātaka (4-3-7)

From the place where my beloved dwells,
This fragrance comes wafting.
My mind is attached to Queen Kākavatī,
Who dwells in a place far from here.

How did you cross the ocean?
How did you cross the Kepuka River?
How did you cross the seven Sīdā oceans?
How did you climb the great silk-cotton tree?

I crossed the ocean with you;
I crossed the Kepuka River with you.
I crossed the seven Sīdā oceans with you;
I climbed the great silk-cotton tree with you.
107:
Shame on me with this large body! Shame on me, the mindless one! For I carried my wife's lover to the Garuda realm and brought him back to the human realm.

## Kākavatī Jātaka is the seventh.

## 328. Ananusociya Jātaka (4-3-8)

Lady, this woman now exists among many others besides me. What connection will she have with me? Therefore, I do not grieve for that beloved, smiling woman.

If one were to grieve for those who have passed away and are no more, one should rather grieve for oneself, who is always falling under the power of Death.

Whether standing, sitting, lying down, or walking, the life-force does not stop following any being. Even in the blink of an eye, youth declines.

When associated with this body, the nature of separation arises without doubt. One should only pity the living being who remains alive. One should not grieve for the dead.

## Ananusociya Jātaka is the eighth.

## 329. Kāḷabāhu Jātaka (4-3-9)

Rādha, the food and drink we used to receive before now go only to the monkey. King Dhanañjaya no longer honors us; let us now go to the forest.

Poṭṭhapāda, gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, happiness and suffering—these conditions among men are impermanent. Why do you grieve? Do not grieve.
108:
Brother Rādha, you are indeed wise; you know the benefits that have not yet come. For what reason shall we see this wicked monkey driven out of the palace?

Younger brother Poṭṭhapāda, this monkey Kāḷabāhu shakes his ears, frowns, and repeatedly frightens the young princesses. For that reason, his food will be endangered and he will be kept far away; he will do this to himself.

## Kāḷabāhu Jātaka, the ninth.

## 330. Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka (4-3-10)

Virtue alone is truly excellent; virtue is supreme in the world.
Look at the snake with fierce poison; because it is virtuous, it is not harmed.

As long as that hawk has a small piece of meat in its beak,
The other hawks in the world gather and peck at it.
But they do not harm one who has no piece of meat to worry about.

One without desire sleeps happily; desire that bears fruit is happy.
Having cut off her longing desire, the slave girl named Piṅgalā sleeps happily.

In this world and in the next, there is no quality higher than concentration.
One who is endowed with concentration harms neither others nor himself.

## Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka, the tenth.

## Kuṭidūsaka Vagga, the third.

The summary of that chapter is:
Samanussa Jātaka, Saduddubha Jātaka, Yācanaka Jātaka, then the noble Meṇḍaka Jātaka and the noble Godha Jātaka, then Kāyasakepuka Jātaka, Bhotīvara Jātaka, then Rādha Jātaka and the noble Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka—these are the ten.
109:
## 4. Kokilavagga
## 331. Kokila Jātaka (4-4-1)
Truly, he who speaks before the proper time and speaks excessively is destroyed and lies dead, just as the offspring of a cuckoo is killed.
Neither a well-sharpened sword nor halāhala poison can kill as instantly as a badly spoken word kills at the very moment it is uttered.
Therefore, a wise person should guard their speech, whether at the right time or the wrong time. They should not speak excessively, even in the presence of an equal.
A wise person who first investigates with wisdom and speaks measured words at the proper time can subdue all enemies, just as a Garuda catches a Naga.
## The Kokila Jātaka [Kokalika Jātaka] is the first.
## 332. Rathalaṭṭhi Jātaka (4-4-2)
O Great King, some people, though they themselves have killed another, will speak first saying, "He is killing me." Though they themselves have won, they say, "I have lost." Therefore, one should not definitely believe the words of the first person who comes to report.
Therefore, a wise person should also listen to the words of the other party. Only after hearing the words of both parties should one make a decision according to the Dhamma.
A layman who enjoys sensual pleasures is not good if he is lazy. A monk is not good if he is unrestrained in body, speech, and mind. A king is not good if he acts without reflection. A wise man is not good if he is prone to anger.
A king should act after investigation. O Great King, one should not act without investigation. The retinue, wealth, and fame of a king who acts with investigation will increase.
## The Rathalaṭṭhi Jātaka is the second.
110:
## 333. Pakkagodha Jātaka (4-4-3)
O Great King, leader of chariot warriors, there was a time when you traveled in the midst of the multitude, wearing a sword, clad in armor, and dressed in bark garments. At that time of travel, without giving me any meat, you said, "The roasted lizard on the branch of the Bodhi tree has fled." Your Majesty should know this situation.
One should respond with a humble heart only to those who are humble towards oneself. One should associate only with those who associate with oneself. One should perform the tasks only of those who look after one's own affairs. One should not seek the welfare of those who do not desire one's own welfare. One should not associate with those who do not associate with oneself.
One should abandon those who abandon oneself. One should not form a forest of craving for those who have discarded oneself. One should not associate with a mind devoid of attachment. Just as a bird, knowing a tree is exhausted of fruit, looks for another tree with fruit, indeed, the world is wide.
O Queen, I, the lord of the land, seeing your gratitude, will act according to my power and strength. I give you all sovereignty. You may give wealth to whomever you desire.
## The Pakkagodha Jātaka is the third.
## 334. Rājovāda Jātaka (4-4-4)
Among cattle crossing a river, if the leader bull goes crookedly, when the leader goes crookedly, all those cows go crookedly.
In the same way, among humans, whoever is considered the chief, if that king practices unrighteousness, the rest of the people will also practice unrighteousness even more so. If the king is unrighteous, the entire country sleeps in suffering.
Among cattle crossing a river, if the leader bull goes straight, when the leader goes straight, all those cows go straight.
111:
In the same way, among humans, there is a king who is considered the chief. If that king practices the Dhamma, the rest of the beings will also practice the Dhamma even more so. If the king is a Dhamma-abiding king, the entire country lives in happiness.
## The Rājovāda Jātaka is finished.
## 335. Jambuka Jātaka (4-4-5)
O Jackal, that elephant has a very large body, a tall stature, and long tusks. You were not born into that race of lions who can catch elephants.
He who, though not a lion, behaves perversely with the pride of a lion, will lie groaning on the ground like a jackal that has attacked a noble elephant.
Without considering the power and strength of the famous, noble, broad-shouldered, and mighty lion, this jackal has been killed by the noble elephant and lies on the ground.
In this world, he who knows his own strength and performs his tasks after investigating through recitation of mantras, consultation, and good speech—such a person succeeds in gaining great benefits.
## The Jambuka Jātaka is finished.
## 336. Brahāchatta Jātaka (4-4-6)
"Grass, grass," you are lamenting. Who took your grass? Do you have any business with grass? Why do you speak of grass again and again?
The student Chatta, who leads a holy life, is large in body and very learned, came here. He took all my wealth and left, leaving only the grass.
One who desires much wealth by giving a little grass should act in this way. Taking all of one's own wealth and leaving the useless grass is what ought to be done. He has left the grass in the pots and gone; why are you lamenting over his departure?
112:
Virtuous people do not perform such base deeds; only the fool practices his own [evil] habits. For one with unstable virtue or no virtue, what benefit can being wise bring?

## Brahāchatta Jātaka, the Sixth.

## 337. Pīṭha Jātaka (4-4-7)

O Venerable One who practices the holy life, we did not offer you a seat, nor drinking water, nor food. I see this fault; please forgive this transgression.

I have no attachment, nor am I angry; no unpleasant thought has arisen in me. Indeed, the thought occurred to me: "Is this the custom of this family?"

This is the custom in our family, always present since the time of our fathers and grandfathers; we offer a seat, drinking water, and water for washing the feet—all of these.

This is the custom in our family, always present since the time of our fathers and grandfathers; we serve [ascetics and brahmins] respectfully, just as we would a noble relative.

## Pīṭha Jātaka, the Seventh.

## 338. Thusa Jātaka (4-4-8)

Rats know the chaff and they know the rice [even in the dark]. Discarding the chaff, they eat only the rice.

The consultation in the forest, the whispering ear-to-ear in the city, and the plan said as "this and that" [to kill me]—all that I know.

By nature, a father monkey bites off the [organ] fruit of his own young son with his teeth while he is still small.

Why do you tremble like a blind goat entering a mustard field? I also know the one who is lying under the throne.

## Thusa Jātaka, the Eighth.
113:
## 339. Bāveru Jātaka (4-4-9)
Because they did not see the peacock king, who has a beautiful voice and is endowed with a crest, the people in that kingdom of Bāveru worshipped a crow with meat and various fruits.

But when the peacock king, endowed with a beautiful voice, arrived in the kingdom of Bāveru, then the gains and honors of the crow diminished.

As long as the Buddha—the King of Dhamma through the nine supramundane states, the maker of light in the three worlds—had not yet appeared, people worshipped many other ascetics and brahmins.

But when the Buddha, endowed with a voice having eight qualities like the voice of Great Brahma, preached the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, then the gains and honors of the heretics diminished.

## Bāveru Jātaka, the Ninth.

## 340. Visayha Jātaka (4-4-10)
O Visayha the merchant, in the time before this, you gave gifts. To you who gave, the nature of the exhaustion of wealth has occurred. If after this time you do not give gifts and maintain them with restraint, your wealth will remain.

O Sakka of a thousand eyes, the Noble Ones of pure conduct say that even if one is extremely poor, the act of not giving is a base deed that should not be done. O King of Devas, let us not have that kind of wealth for the sake of which we would abandon faith.

O Vāsava Sakka, just as another chariot travels by the path taken by one chariot, the practice of giving established by the virtuous of old continues even until now.

If there is wealth, we shall give; if there is no wealth, what can we give? Even while living in poverty by cutting grass, we shall give; let us not be heedless in giving.

## Visayha Jātaka, the Tenth.

## Kokila Vagga, the Fourth.
114:
The summary verses of that chapter:
The King Jītavara who shines exceedingly, King Rathesabha with a noble chariot in the middle of the forest, the snake that moves crookedly, then the Jambu fruit, the grass mat and the fine seat, then Taṇḍula (rice), the peacock, Visayha the merchant, and the ten [brahmins].

## 5. Cūḷakuṇāla Vagga
## 341. Kaṇḍarī Jātaka (4-5-1)
In women who bring delight to men, who have many minds, and who are difficult to restrain by punishment, even if they should bring pleasure in all things, one should not be intimate with them. For women are like river landings.

One should see and know the story of the Kinnara king and the Kinnarī queen. All women do not delight in their husband's home. That Kinnarī queen, having abandoned such a Kinnara king, saw another man, a cripple, [and committed misconduct].

Indeed, even the wives of King Baka and King Bāvarika, who followed the pursuit of sensual pleasures, committed base conduct with those who followed their own will. What other woman would not transgress against another man?

Queen Piṅgiyānī, the beloved wife of King Brahmadatta, the ruler of the whole world, also committed base conduct with a groom who followed her will. That queen, though desiring sensual pleasures, failed to get both and met with ruin.

## Kaṇḍarī Jātaka, the First.
115:
## 342. Vānara Jātaka (4-5-2)
O water-dweller (crocodile), I have indeed been able to lift myself from the water to the dry land. Now I shall no longer come under your power.

I have no need for those mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits on the other side of the river. For me, the cluster-fig (udumbara) is much better.

If a person does not quickly perceive a matter or situation that has arisen, that person falls under the power of the enemy and later repents.

If a person quickly perceives a matter or situation that has arisen, that person is released from the enemy's oppression and does not repent later.

## Vānara Jātaka, the second.

## 343. Kuntinī Jātaka (4-5-3)
Great King, we have always lived in your palace, being honored and worshipped. But now you yourself, through heedlessness, have caused me sorrow. Pray, O King, let me go; I shall depart.

O crane, when a person performs a counter-deed against a harsh deed done by another, the enmity is appeased by such retaliation. Therefore, stay, Kuntinī, do not go yet.

O best among charioteers, the friendship between the oppressed and the oppressor cannot be joined again. For that reason, my heart no longer delights in staying here; I shall surely depart.

O crane, the friendship between the oppressed and the oppressor can be joined again for the wise, but not for the foolish. Therefore, stay, Kuntinī, do not go yet.

## Kuntinī Jātaka, the third.

## 344. Amba Jātaka (4-5-4)
O ascetic, may the woman who stole your mangoes follow the will of a grey-headed old man who dyes his white hair black and exerts himself with tweezers to pluck them.

O ascetic, may the woman who stole your mangoes, though she reaches the age of twenty, twenty-five, or twenty-nine from birth, not find a husband at such an age.
116:
O ascetic, may that woman who stole your mangoes become an abhisārikā (a woman seeking a lover), traveling a long distance alone in longing. And may she not see her husband at the appointed place.

O ascetic, may that woman who stole your mangoes, though adorned, well-dressed, wearing garlands, and smeared with sandalwood, sleep alone on her bed without a husband.

## Amba Jātaka [Ambacora Jātaka], the fourth.

## 345. Gajakumbha Jātaka (4-5-5)

When the fire with its black trail burns the forest, O Gajakumbha who moves tremulously, what will you do with such slow effort?

There are many hollows in trees and holes in the ground. If we cannot reach those holes, it will be the time of our death.

He who acts quickly in a time when one should be slow, and acts slowly in a time when one should be quick, destroys his own welfare like one treading upon and crushing a dry leaf.

He who acts slowly in a time when one should be slow, and acts quickly in a time when one should be quick, his welfare becomes full like the moon filling up during the night.

## Gajakumbha Jātaka, the fifth.

## 346. Kesava Jātaka (4-5-6)

Having left the King of Bārāṇasī, the lord of men who is endowed with all sensual pleasures, why, O Blessed Kesava, do you delight in the hermitage of Kappa?

Nārada, in Kappa's hermitage, there are good and delightful trees that are pleasing to the heart. Kappa's well-spoken words delight me.

While you could eat fine rice with pure meat broth, why does the saltless food of sāmāka and nīvāra (millet and wild grain) satisfy you?

Whether it be delicious or not, whether it be little or much, where one eats with trust (vissattha), that trust is the supreme flavor.

## Kesava Jātaka [Kesī Jātaka], the sixth.
117:
## 347. Ayakūṭa Jātaka (4-5-7)
O Yakkha, standing in the sky holding a massive club made entirely of iron, were you appointed to protect me, or are you striving to kill me?

O King, I am a messenger of the Rakkhasas here; I have been sent to kill you. But Sakka, the King of Gods, protects you; therefore, I cannot split your head.

If Maghavā Sujampati, the King of Gods, protects me, let all the Pisācas shout as much as they wish; I am not afraid of those Rakkhasa creatures.

Let the Kumbhaṇḍas and all the dust-Pisācas cry out as much as they wish; those Pisācas are not capable of fighting me. That shouting is merely to cause great terror.

## Ayakūṭa Jātaka, the seventh.

## 348. Arañña Jātaka (4-5-8)
Father, having come from the forest to the village, what kind of virtue and what kind of conduct should a man have for me to associate with him? Please tell me this when asked.

Dear son, when you go from this forest, associate with one who makes you feel at home (trusts you), who tolerates your intimacy, who is willing to listen, and who is patient.

Associate with one who has no evil deed done by body, speech, or mind, like a child resting on the breast, when you go from this forest.
118:
Dear son, do not associate with a man of such a nature—whose mind is as fickle as turmeric dye, as restless as a monkey's, and who is easily moved to love or hate—even if it be in a place deserted by all people.

## Arañña Jātaka, the Eighth.

## 349. Sandhibheda Jātaka (4-5-9)

Charioteer, between this lion and this bull, there is no commonality regarding females, nor is there any commonality regarding food. Yet, look at the destruction so meticulously planned by this backbiting jackal.

Just as a sharp sword cuts through flesh, so does slander arise to sever friendship. Because of that slander, the wretched jackals get to feast upon the king bull and the king lion.

Charioteer, he who believes the words of a backbiting slanderer without investigation will surely lie dead, just like this lion and bull you see here.

Charioteer, those who do not believe the words of a backbiting slanderer to be true attain happiness, like those who have gone to the heavenly realm.

## Sandhibheda Jātaka, the Ninth.

## 350. Devatāpañha Jātaka (4-5-10)

Great King, he strikes with hands and feet, and he strikes the face as well. Yet, he is indeed dearly beloved. Who do you perceive with your wisdom to be the one beloved despite such striking?

He reviles as he pleases, yet his coming is desired. He is indeed dearly beloved. For what reason do you perceive with your wisdom that he is beloved?

He accuses with what is not true, and makes one remember with false words. He is indeed dearly beloved. For what reason do you perceive with your wisdom that he is beloved?

They carry away rice, drink, clothing, and bedding. Even though they are indeed takers, they are dearly beloved. For what reason do you perceive with your wisdom that they are beloved?

## Devatāpañha Jātaka, the Tenth.

## 5. Pañcaka Nipāta

## 1. Maṇikuṇḍala Vagga

## 351. Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka (5-1-1)

Noble King, your majesty has lost (relinquished) the jeweled earrings along with the chariot horses; likewise, you have lost your son and wife. Having lost all possessions without exception, why do you remain steady as usual without burning with grief in this time of sorrow?

O King who desires the five sensual pleasures, wealth often leaves the owner even before the owner dies, or the owner leaves the wealth first (by dying). Wealth-owners are not eternal; therefore, I do not grieve in this time of sorrow.

The moon rises, becomes full, and wanes. The sun, having destroyed the darkness (shining with heat), goes to its setting. O enemy king, I have understood the worldly conditions (lokadhamma); therefore, I do not grieve in this time of sorrow.

A householder who enjoys pleasures is not good if lazy; a monk is not good if unrestrained; a king is not good if he acts without reflection; and if a wise person is prone to anger, he is not good.

A Khattiya should act with reflection and investigation; a king who is the lord of the quarters should not act without reflection. Great King, the retinue and fame of a king who acts with reflection will increase.

## Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka, the First.
121:
Why, as if in a great hurry, having mown green grass, do you say to a dead old ox, "Eat, eat"? A dead ox cannot rise even if given food or water. Just as an ignorant person would speak, so do you speak empty words.

(The son Sujāta replied:) Father, the head remains just as it was before. The hands and feet also remain just so. The tail also remains just so. Since the ox remains just as it was, I thought that the ox should rise. The head of my grandfather, as well as his hands and feet, are not visible at all. This being so, is it not you, father, who are ignorant for weeping at an earth mound?

(The father praised him:) Indeed, just as one would extinguish a fire fed with ghee by pouring water on it, so has my dear son Sujāta extinguished me who was burning with the fire of grief. He has extinguished all grief that causes the mind to suffer. This son Sujāta has indeed pulled out the arrow of sorrow that was lodged in my heart, the grief caused by the death of my father which oppressed me.

Young man, by hearing your words, I have become one whose arrow of grief is pulled out. I am free from sorrow, free from mental turbidity. Now I no longer grieve, I no longer weep. Just as the wise, who are compassionate, turn Sujāta's father away from grief, so do they turn others away from sorrow.

## Sujāta Jātaka, the Second.

## 353. Veṇasākha Jātaka (5-1-3)

Prince Brahmadatta, for these beings, safety, abundance of food, and physical comfort are not eternal. When your own power, wealth, and happiness decline, do not be greatly bewildered and despondent, like a man whose boat is wrecked in the middle of the ocean and finds no refuge.
122:
Whatever deeds a man does, those he sees in himself. The doer of good sees good, and the doer of evil sees evil. Whatever kind of seed one sows, such is the fruit one reaps.

This is the word of the teacher, which the noble teacher Pārāsariya spoke: "Do not do evil, which you will later regret."

This is that very banyan tree with spreading branches where I slaughtered a thousand khattiyas. That very suffering (caused by killing them) has now come back to me, even though I was adorned and anointed with the essence of sandalwood.

And my Queen Ubbarī, whose body is anointed with sandalwood, who is as beautiful and trembling as a fresh sprout of the drumstick tree (sobhāñjana) rising upwards—I shall die without seeing her. Not seeing her will be more painful to me than this death itself.

## Venasākha Jātaka, the third.

## 354. Uraga Jātaka (5-1-4)

Just as a snake sheds its old skin and goes on, so it is when the body becomes useless and the deceased passes away (the consciousness leaves the old body).

He who is being cremated does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; he has gone to the destination according to his own kamma.

Uninvited he came from that life, and without taking leave he departed from here. As he came, so he went; what use is there in lamenting his departure?

He who is being cremated does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; he has gone to the destination according to his own kamma.

If I were to weep and grow thin, what benefit would there be for me? It would only cause more distress to our relatives and friends.
123:
He who is being cremated does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; he has gone to his own destination.

Just as a child cries for the moon that moves across the sky, so is the state of one who grieves for the dead.

He who is being cremated does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; he has gone to his own destination.

Just as a broken water pot cannot be joined back together, so is the state of one who grieves for the dead.

He who is being cremated does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; he has gone to his own destination.

## Uraga Jātaka, the fourth.

## 355. Ghaṭa Jātaka (5-1-5)

Other people grieve and weep, their faces drenched in tears. But you, King Ghaṭa, have a serene countenance; why do you not grieve?

Grief cannot bring back past benefits, nor can it bring future happiness. Therefore, King Ghaṭa, I do not grieve; there is no helpful benefit in grieving.

One who grieves becomes pale and thin, and has no appetite for food. When enemies see one suffering, pierced by the arrow of grief, they rejoice.

Whether in a village or a forest, in a valley or on high ground, destruction (born of grief) cannot come to me; thus, I am one who has seen the truth.

If a person does not have even a single friend who can bring all desired pleasures, then even the whole earth will not be able to bring him happiness.

## Ghaṭa Jātaka, the fifth.
124:
## 356. Koraṇḍiya Jātaka (5-1-6)
O Koraṇḍiya, why are you alone in the forest, lifting and throwing rocks into the mountain cleft with such great haste? What benefit do you gain by throwing rocks like this?

I shall make this great earth, bounded by the four oceans, as level as the palm of a hand by spreading out the hills and mountains. That is why I am throwing rocks into the cleft.

Koraṇḍiya, no one is able to make this earth level by hand. I think you will depart from this world of men without even being able to fill this single cleft.

O Brahmin teacher, if I, being but one person, cannot make the earth that supports all beings level, then in the same way, you will not be able to guide these people of various views to your will by admonishing them to "take these precepts."

Koraṇḍiya, you have explained the matter to me with a brief simile. It is just as you say. Just as one person cannot make the earth level, so one person cannot make all people uniform.

## Koraṇḍiya Jātaka, the sixth.

## 357. Laṭukika Jātaka (5-1-7)
I pay homage to you, O elephant king, sixty years of age, tireless, roaming the forest, the glorious leader of the herd. I salute you with my wings joined in reverence. Do not kill my weak little offspring.
125:
O King Elephant, who wanders alone, who dwells in the forest, who seeks food on the mountain slopes, I pay homage to you. With both wings, I join my hands in reverence. Do not kill my weak little offspring.

Little quail, I shall kill your young. You are very weak; what can you do to me? Even a hundred thousand like you, I would crush with my left foot.

O King Elephant, not everything can be accomplished by physical strength alone. The strength of a fool is only for his own destruction. O King Elephant, who killed my weak little offspring, I shall bring about your ruin.

Monks, look at the crow, the little quail, the frog, and the black fly. These creatures were able to kill the great tusker. Behold the result of vengeance upon enemies. Therefore, one should not create enmity, even with one who is disliked.

## Laṭukika Jātaka, the Seventh.

## 358. Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka (5-1-8)

Great King Mahāpatāpa, I alone am the foolish woman who has offended the Great King. I alone am the destroyer of my own welfare. Please release this young boy Dhammapāla; Great King, please cut off only my hands.

Great King Mahāpatāpa, I alone am the foolish woman who has offended the Great King. I alone am the destroyer of my own welfare. Please release this young boy Dhammapāla; Great King, please cut off only my feet.

Great King Mahāpatāpa, I alone am the foolish woman who has offended the Great King. I alone am the destroyer of my own welfare. Please release this young boy Dhammapāla; Great King, please cut off only my head.

Are there indeed no good friends, no good ministers, no good-hearted people for this Great King, who would forbid him, saying, "Do not kill your own son, your own flesh and blood"?

Are there indeed no good kinsmen, no good friends, no good-hearted people for this Great King, who would forbid him, saying, "Do not kill your own son, born of yourself"?
126:
O Great King, the two arms of Dhammapāla, anointed with sandalwood essence, the heir to the earth bounded by the four oceans, are severed. O Great King, my life-force is coming to an end.

## Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, the Eighth.

## 359. Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka (5-1-9)

O my dear husband, King of Deer, with feet like the color of gold, strive! O my dear husband, the noble King of Deer, strive! Cut the snare made of leather thongs. Separated from my dear husband, I cannot delight in the forest alone.

Lady, I am striving with effort. However, I am unable to break the snare. I kick the ground with force. The snare made of leather thongs is very firm. It is cutting all around my foot.

Hunter, spread out the leaves. Draw the sword from its sheath. Kill me first, and then kill the noble King of Deer.

Never before this have I seen or heard of a doe that speaks the language of humans. O wise lady, may you be happy. May this noble King of Deer, your dear husband, also be happy.

Hunter, just as I am joyful today seeing the noble King of Deer freed from the snare, so may you also be joyful together with all your kinsmen.

## Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka, the Ninth.

## 360. Suyonandī Jātaka (5-1-10)

King Tamba, in the Garuda realm far from this city of Bārāṇasī, dwells the queen named Suyonandī. In that place, the scent of Timira flowers spreads. The small ocean named Kusa also roars loudly. Sensual desires pierce me.

Sagga, by what means did you cross the ocean? By what means did you see the island of Seruma? How did the meeting between that Suyonandī and you occur?

The ship of the merchants seeking wealth, who set out from the port of Kurukaccha, was wrecked by sea monsters. I crossed by means of a plank.
127:
That lovely Queen Sussondī, constantly anointed with sandalwood perfume, lifted me with her two arms, just as a mother lifts the son born of her breast, with smooth and gentle words.

King Tamba, know that the queen of gentle manners made me delighted and content with divine food, divine drink, divine clothing, and a divine bed, as well as with her own self.

## Suyonandī Jātaka (the Tenth) ends.

## Maṇikuṇḍala Vagga (the First) ends.

The summary of that Vagga is: Jinavara, Harita, Tiṇa, Bhinnaplava, Uraga, Ghaṭa, Dari, Kuñjara, Bhūnahata, and Migamuttama (Saggavara)—these are the ten Jātakas.

## 2. Vaṇṇāroha Vagga

## 361. Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka (5-2-1)

King Lion, do you say that the tiger named Subāhu is not superior or better than me in appearance, in birth, or in strength and effort?

King Tiger, do you say that the lion named Sudāṭha is not superior or better than me in appearance, in birth, or in strength and effort?

Friend Subāhu, if you harbor malice against me who lives in harmony with you, I no longer delight in living together with you.

Whoever believes the words of others as the truth will quickly be divided from friends and will increase much enmity.
128:
He who is always heedful, fearing a breach of friendship and constantly looking for faults, is not a friend.

He in whom one can sleep as trustfully as a child in its mother's breast, and who cannot be divided by others, he is indeed a true friend.

## Vaᅉᅉāroha Jātaka, the first.

## 362. Sĩlavĩmaᅃsa Jātaka (5-2-2)
I once had a doubt: 'Is virtue better, or is learning (suta) better?' Now I have no doubt: 'Virtue alone is better than learning.'

Birth and appearance are useless; virtue alone is truly supreme. For one who is not endowed with virtue, learning is of no benefit.

A king who does not stand in righteousness and a merchant who relies on unrighteousness—both of them, having left this world, go to a state of misery (duggati).

Khattiyas, Brahmins, Vessas, Suddas, Caᅉᅡālas, and Pukkusas—if they practice the Dhamma in this life, they become equal in the heavenly realm.

Neither the Vedas, nor birth, nor kinsmen are capable for the life hereafter. Only one's own pure virtue leads to happiness in the life hereafter.

## Sĩlavĩmaᅃsa Jātaka, the second.

## 363. Hiri Jātaka (5-2-3)
One who transgresses shame (hiri), loathing friendship, and merely says 'I am your friend' but does not perform noble deeds—one should know him as 'This man is not my friend.'

What one can do, that alone should one say. What one cannot do, that one should not say. The wise recognize the one who speaks without doing.
129:
He who is always fearing a breach of friendship and constantly looking for faults is not a friend. He in whom one can sleep as trustfully as a child in its mother's breast, and who cannot be divided by others, he is indeed a true friend.

Seeing the benefits, he who carries out the duties of a man cultivates the association of good friends (kalyāᅉamitta) who cause joy, bring praise, and are the cause of happiness.

By drinking the taste of seclusion and the taste of the calming of defilements, he who drinks the taste of joy in the Dhamma (dhammapĩti) becomes free from distress and free from evil.

## Hiri Jātaka is the third.

## 364. Khajjopanaka Jātaka (5-2-4)
Who, while there is a bright fire, goes searching for fire? Seeing a firefly at night, he thought it was fire.

With a perverted perception, he scattered cow-dung powder and grass over that firefly, but he could not make it burn.

Thus, just as one does not get milk by milking a cow's horn, a foolish person cannot obtain benefit through wrong means.

Men attain benefits through various means, such as by suppressing enemies and by supporting friends.

By obtaining a good general and by the guidance of beloved ministers, kings who protect the earth rule over this world.

## Khajjopanaka Jātaka is the fourth.

## 365. Ahituᅉᅡika Jātaka (5-2-5)
Friend Sumukha, I am a gambler who has been defeated in the game of dice. Bring the ripe mangoes; depending on your effort, let us eat.

Friend, you are indeed praising me with false words. Where have you ever heard of or seen a monkey named Sumukha (Beautiful-faced)?
131:
If a person desires to kill one who does not harm or strike them, and who does not deserve to be harmed or killed, that person will lie down slain, just as this physician lies slain. 

Just as a man throwing a handful of dust against the wind finds that the dust returns to strike only him, so too this physician lies down afflicted. 

Whoever offends against an innocent person, pure and free from defilements, that evil returns to that fool, like fine dust thrown against the wind.

## The Seventh, Sāḷiya Jātaka.

## 368. Tacasāra Jātaka (5-2-8)

Though you have fallen into the hands of enemies and are firmly bound with bamboo, why do you not grieve and instead have such bright countenances?

Not even a small benefit can be gained through grieving or lamentation. Seeing one who is sorrowful and suffering, enemies become delighted.

When a wise person, who knows how to determine what is beneficial, encounters misfortunes, they do not tremble. Seeing their face unchanged and as it was before, the enemies themselves fall into suffering.

By means of incantations, mantras, wise counsel, pleasant speech, giving gifts, or by citing lineage—by whatever means and in whatever place one might gain a benefit, one should exert effort in that way and in that place.
132:
When one realizes that this benefit cannot be attained by oneself or by another, despite various efforts, then the wise person, without a darkened face, remaining steady and without grief, should endure it, reflecting: "The unwholesome kamma committed in the past is indeed firm; it cannot be warded off or prevented. What can I do now?"

## The Tacasāra Jātaka is the eighth.

## 369. Mittavindaka Jātaka (5-2-9)

O divine being, what have I done to the gods? What evil have I committed, that this razor-wheel presses upon my head and spins upon my brow?

Having passed the Ramanaka (crystal) palace, the Sadāmatta (silver) palace, the Dūbhaka (ruby) palace, and the Brahmattara (golden) palace, for what reason did you come to this hell?

O divine being, I thought that in this place there would be wealth and happiness far greater than in those four palaces. Look at me, who has come to ruin by coming here with such a wrong perception.

You obtained four nymphs, then eight; from eight you obtained sixteen. From sixteen you obtained thirty-two. Not being content with what you had, and having great lust for sensual objects, you have reached the razor-wheel. The razor-wheel spins upon the head of a man oppressed by greed.

Craving, which delights in sensual objects, is vast above and difficult to fill; it tends toward expansion. Those who repeatedly lust after and grasp that craving are the ones who bear the razor-wheel.

## The Mittavindaka Jātaka is the ninth.

## 370. Palāsa Jātaka (5-2-10)

The Golden Goose King said this to the Palāsa tree spirit: "Friend Palāsa spirit, a banyan tree is growing, established in the fork of your branches. When that banyan tree grows large, it will, like an enemy, sever your life-sustaining roots."

"Friend Goose King, let the banyan tree grow; I shall be the support of that banyan tree. Just as parents are the support of their children, so too shall that banyan tree be my support."

"O spirit, you are allowing a terrifying, milk-producing banyan tree to grow in the fork of your branches. Therefore, we shall inform you and depart; I do not like the growth of that banyan tree."
133:
Now this banyan tree causes me fear; not knowing and not following the firm and great words of the Goose King, which are like Mount Meru, great danger has come upon me.

The growth of that which, when it arises, destroys its own support, is not praised by the wise. A wise person, fearing the destruction caused by such a thing, endeavors to destroy it along with its roots.

## The tenth, Palāsa Jātaka.

## 3. Aḍḍha Vagga

## 371. Dīghītikosala Jātaka (5-3-1)

Great King, for your majesty who has fallen into my hands and reached such a state, is there any means that can release you from this suffering?

Dear son, for me who has fallen into your hands and reached such a state, there is no means that can release me from this suffering.

Great King, at the time of death, I see no other protective Dhamma than the good conduct which is the instruction given by parents. Other wealth, even amounting to hundreds or thousands of crores, is simply of no benefit.

"He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me"—in those who harbor such enmity, hatred is never appeased.

"He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me"—in those who do not harbor such enmity, hatred is appeased.

For in this world, hatred is never appeased by hatred; it is appeased only by non-hatred. This is an ancient and eternal law.

## The first, Dīghītikosala Jātaka.

## 372. Migapotaka Jātaka (5-3-2)

For you, who have left the home to become a monk, free from the affairs of householders, it is not good that you are grieving and lamenting for one who has passed away (the young deer).
134:
O Sakka, through living together, whether with a human or a beast, love truly arises in the heart; one cannot help but grieve for the beloved.

Those who weep and wail cry for the dead and for those who will die. Therefore, O ascetic, do not weep; the virtuous say that weeping is in vain.

O ascetic, if by weeping the dead could rise again, we would all gather and weep for one another's kinsmen.

Just as one extinguishes a fire fed with ghee by pouring water on it, so has Sakka truly extinguished all my burning grief.

Sakka, who removed the sorrow for my son, has truly plucked out the arrow of grief that rested in my heart.

I, with the arrow plucked out, am free from sorrow and untroubled. O Sakka, having heard your words, I no longer grieve nor weep.

## The Migapotaka Jātaka is the second.

## 373. Mūsika Jātaka (5-3-3)

"Where has the mouse gone? Where has she gone?" so the people lament. I alone know that the mouse was killed in the well.

I know you are wandering here and there like a donkey, looking for an opportunity to kill. Having killed the mouse in the well, do you now wish to kill me, the barley-king, today?

O unwise prince, though you are young and in the first stage of life, you hold and brandish this long ladle. I shall not give you your life today.

I was not saved from the danger of death by living in a celestial mansion, nor by the love of a son who is like my own limbs. Indeed, my beloved son plotted to kill me. I was saved from death only because of the verses given by my teacher.

One should learn all branches of knowledge—low, high, or middle. One should understand the meaning of everything, but one should not apply everything at all times. There is a time when learning brings about one's benefit.

## The Mūsika Jātaka is the third.
135:
## 374. Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka (5-3-4)

O Brahmin, you have taken all the goods and crossed to the other shore. Now, come back quickly from that shore and let me cross as well.

O Brahmin woman, you exchanged your long-standing husband for me, whom you have never associated with before. You exchanged a permanent husband for me, who is impermanent. You will surely exchange me for another husband as well. I shall go to a place far away from here.

What woman is laughing so loudly in this clump of kusa grass? There is no dancing or singing here, nor the sound of well-played hand-clapping, drums, or cymbals. O lady of beautiful form and fine hips, why do you laugh so loudly at an improper time?

O foolish and unwise jackal, you have little wisdom. Having lost both the fish and the piece of meat, you brood miserably like one who has lost a thousand pieces of gold.

O base woman, the faults of others are easy to see, but one's own faults are hard to perceive. I think you shall brood and grieve a thousand times more than I, having lost both the husband given by your father and the husband you took on the road.

O jackal, king of beasts, what you say is true. If I go from here and find another husband, I shall certainly live according to his will.

He who steals a clay bowl will also steal a bronze bowl. You have committed this evil before, and you will surely commit such evil again.

## The Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka is the fourth.

## 375. Kapota Jātaka (5-3-5)

Now I am happy and healthy; I am free from thorns, and the pigeon has departed. Now I shall satisfy my heart's desire. That meat curry seems to urge me to make an effort.
136:
Who is this female crane with a crest, who steals a good place, and whose price is the rain? O crane, come inside. My friend the crow is fierce.

Friend, it is not right for you to mock me, seeing me in such great misery, with my feathers plucked clean by the cook's son and smeared with a paste of ginger and mustard.

Friend, you are well-bathed and well-anointed, and you are satisfied with food and drink. You also wear a beryl gem around your neck. Have you been to the region of Kajangala without showing yourself to me for all this time?

O pigeon, do not let anyone, whether friend or foe, go to the region of Kajangala. There, they pluck out the feathers and tie a potsherd around the neck.

Friend, you will fall into such misery again. Truly, your habit is of such a base nature that leads to suffering. The belongings of humans are not easily enjoyed by birds.
