Now I shall go to the edges of the forest as I please. Such dead ones cannot be friends. While I am alive, I can find new friends.

One who associates with a wicked friend never attains lasting happiness. Behold Manoja lying dead, having followed the advice of a jackal.

Because of associating with a wicked friend, a mother does not rejoice because of her son. Behold Manoja lying dead, immersed in his own blood.

Whosoever does not listen to or follow the words of those who see the benefit and desire his welfare, such a person reaches the suffering of death and meets with evil.

And he becomes even more wretched than that, he who is noble yet associates with a person of base conduct. Behold the noble king of lions, Manoja, who, despite being great in physical strength, was pierced by the force of an arrow because he associated with one of base conduct.
157:
A man who associates with the base becomes base; one who associates with equals never declines; one who resorts to the superior quickly rises in virtues such as morality. Therefore, one should associate with those who are superior to oneself.

## Manojajātaka, the Second.

## 398. Sutanujātaka (7-1-3)

O deity residing in the banyan tree, the king has sent you rice together with pure meat curry. Come out and eat!

Young man, come this way, bringing the regular meal for me, which is complete with savory dishes. Young man, are you not also my food? Both you and the rice shall become my food.

O Yakkha, for a small reason you will sacrifice a great benefit. People, perceiving that they will die, will no longer bring rice to you.

O Yakkha, if you receive your regular meal which is pure, excellent, and full of flavor, it is to your benefit. But if you eat me, a man who brings and offers rice to you here will be very hard to find.

Young man Sutanu, this benefit is indeed for my own welfare, just as you say. I grant you permission; go safely and see your mother.

Young man, take the sword, the parasol, and the golden platter and go. May your mother see you safe and sound, and may you also see your mother.

O Yakkha, may you thus be happy along with all your kinsfolk. I have also obtained wealth, and the king's command has been fulfilled.

## Sutanujātaka, the Third.
158:
## 399. Mātuposakagijjha Jātaka (7-1-4)

(1011) "I have been bound by a snare and have fallen into the hands of the hunter. How will my very aged parents, dwelling in the mountain cave, survive?"

(1012) "Vulture, why do you lament? What is the nature of your lamentation? I have never heard or seen a bird speaking the language of humans."

(1013) "Hunter, I am one who supports my very aged parents who dwell in the mountain cave. If I have fallen into your hands, how will those parents survive?"

(1014) "It is said in the world that a vulture can see carcasses from a distance of a hundred leagues. This being so, why did you not perceive the net and snare set for your own harm, even when you reached them?"

(1015) "Hunter, when beings reach the end of their lives and encounter destruction, then they cannot perceive even the net and snare set for their own harm, though they have reached them."

(1016) "O King of Vultures, go and support your very aged parents dwelling in the mountain cave. I grant you permission. Go in safety to your kinsfolk."

(1017) "Hunter, just as I rejoice at being freed from the jaws of death, may you also rejoice with all your kinsfolk. I shall support my very aged parents dwelling in the mountain cave."

## The Mātuposakagijjha Jātaka, the fourth.

## 400. Dabbhapuppha Jātaka (7-1-5)

(1018) "Friend otter who wanders along the bank, may it be well with you. My Rohita fish is very large; that fish is pulling me away with great force. Friend, follow me and help."

(1019) "Friend otter who wanders in deep water, may it be well with you. Hold on firmly with all your strength. I will pull up that fish, just as a Garuḍa carries off a Nāga."

(1020) "Friend Dabbhapuppha, listen to my words. A dispute has arisen between us. Please settle this dispute so that it may be appeased."

(1021) "Friend otter, in the past, I was a great judicial minister of a king established in Dhamma. I have settled many cases. I shall appease your dispute. Relying on me, may your dispute be settled."

(1022) "Let the otter who goes along the bank take the tail portion. Let the otter who goes in deep water take the head portion. The remaining middle portion shall be for the judge."
159:
"Let the otter who goes along the bank take the tail portion; let the otter who goes in deep water take the head portion. This middle portion, remaining after the tail and head, shall be for me, the jackal who is the judge."

"If we had not quarreled, we would have had food to eat for a long time, even for two or three days. But now, the jackal has carried away the Rohita fish meat, including the middle belly, without the head-bone or tail-bone."

"Just as a Khattiya king who has gained kingship rejoices, so do I rejoice today, seeing my husband with his mouth full of fish."

"Friend, though you are a land-dweller, how did you catch a fish that is in the water? Tell me what I ask; how did you obtain that fish?"

"My dear, these beings become lean because of disputes; because of disputes, their wealth and property are exhausted. These two otters, because of their dispute, have had to give up this Rohita fish meat. O Māyāvī, my dear, eat this Rohita fish meat."

"Monks, in the same way among humans, wherever a dispute arises, they run to one who will judge. That judge is their refuge who removes their stains. In that dispute, wealth is lost, and the king's treasury increases."

## The Dabbhapuppha Jātaka, the fifth.

## 401. Paṇṇaka Jātaka (7-1-6)

"O wise one, a man swallows a sword made in the Paṇṇaka country, sharp-edged and well-polished (or possessing the marks of a great sword), in the midst of an assembly. Is there any deed more difficult than that sword-swallowing? Tell me of another difficult matter that I ask."

"A man may swallow a well-polished sword out of greed. But if one should say, 'I will give,' that saying is much more difficult than swallowing a sword. O King Maddava, know that all other matters are easy."

"Ayura, who is skilled in Dhamma, has answered the meaning of the question. Now I ask Pukkusa: Is there any deed more difficult than saying 'I will give'? Tell me of another difficult matter that I ask."
160:
O King Maddava, beings do not live by uttering fruitless words. More difficult than saying one will give is not wavering (not regretting) after having given. Know that everything else is easy.

Pukkusa, who is skilled in the Dhamma, has answered the meaning of the question. Now I shall ask Senaka: what is more difficult than that? Being asked, tell me another difficult matter.

A man should give a gift, whether it be small or great. More difficult than that giving is not feeling regret (not worrying) afterwards. O King Maddava, know that everything else is easy.

Ayura and Pukkusa have answered the question. As Senaka speaks, his words surpass all the questions.

## 6. Paṇṇaka Jātaka is finished.

## 402. Sattubhasta Jātaka (7-1-7)

Brahmin, you have a disturbed mind and impaired faculties; tears are flowing from your eyes. What have you lost, or what do you desire, that you have come here? Brahmin, tell me that reason.

The yakkha said that if I go home today, my wife shall die; if I do not go, I shall die. I am trembling because of this suffering. O Wise Senaka, tell me about this matter.

After considering many reasons, only what I say here is the truth. Brahmin, I think that a cobra has entered your bag of flour without your knowledge.
161:
Take a staff and strike the bag; look at the snake that spits, is double-tongued, and crawls on its breast. Today, cut off your doubts and recurring uncertainties; look at the snake and untie the bag.

In the midst of the assembly, that brahmin, appearing terrified, untied the bag. Then the snake, of fierce power and swift poison, crawling on its breast, came out with its hood raised.

King Janaka, who beholds the wise minister Senaka, has attained a great gain. Brahmin, are you one who has removed the veil of defilements and sees all things? Is your wisdom of such an extraordinary nature?

I have these seven hundred coins; take them all, I give them to you. Today you have given me my life, and you have also brought well-being to my wife.

The wise do not take a fee for verses that are ornate and well-spoken. Brahmin, let them give you wealth from my presence as well; take it and go to your own home.

## 7. Sattubhasta Jātaka is finished.

## 403. Aṭṭhisena Jātaka (7-1-8)

Venerable Aṭṭhisena, those beggars whom I do not know come to me in unison and ask. Why do you not ask of me?

One who begs becomes unloved (by the giver); one who does not give what is begged also becomes unloved (by the beggar). Therefore, so that I may not be disliked, I do not ask of you.
162:
If a recluse or brahmin who lives by begging does not beg when it is the proper time to beg, he causes another to fall away from merit, and he himself does not live happily.

If a recluse or brahmin who lives by begging begs when it is the proper time to beg, he causes another to gain merit, and he himself lives happily.

The wise who know the nature of giving and its fruits do not get angry or feel hatred when they see beggars coming to them. They invite them, saying: 'Venerable one of noble conduct, you are dear to me; please speak whatever word you desire.'

The wise and virtuous do not beg rudely (saying, 'Give me this wealth'). The steady and wise donor should also know what is needed. The Noble Ones stand silently for the sake of what is needed, following the custom of collecting alms (without speaking); such standing itself is called the begging of the Noble Ones.

O monk who has discarded evil, I donate to you a thousand red cows along with a leading bull. Having heard your verses endowed with Dhamma, why should I, being a Noble One in conduct, not give to you, who are also a Noble One in conduct?

## 8. Aṭṭhisena Jātaka is finished.

## 404. Kapi Jātaka (7-1-9)

A wise person should not live in a place where an enemy dwells. Living among enemies for even one or two days is very painful.

An enemy indeed arises for one who is light-minded or for one who follows the example of the light-minded. Because of a single light-minded monkey, the entire troop of monkeys came to ruin.

A fool who considers himself wise and leads a group, by following the whims of his own mind, will be seen dead just like this monkey.

A powerful fool who leads a group is not good. Like a decoy bird that catches other birds, he brings harm to his own kinsmen.
163:
Only a wise person who is strong and capable of leading his companions is good. Like Sakka, the king of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, he brings about the welfare of his relatives.

And he who sees virtue, wisdom, and learning within himself can work for both his own benefit and the benefit of others.

Therefore, just as one weighs virtue, wisdom, and learning, one should also weigh oneself in those qualities of virtue, wisdom, and learning. Having weighed them, a wise person should either lead a group or practice alone.

## The Ninth, Kapi Jātaka.

## 405. Baka Jātaka (7-1-10)

O Gautama, we seventy-two who possess meritorious deeds are masters of our own will, having transcended birth and old age. This birth in the Brahma realm, attained by the wise, is the final birth. Many beings long for us, wishing they could live as long as we do.

O Baka Brahma, you think this life is long, but it is very short; in truth, it is not long. O Brahma, I know your life is only as long as one hundred thousand nirabbuda and ahaha numbers.

O Gautama, they say you are the Buddha who sees the infinite Dhamma, one who has transcended birth, old age, and sorrow. If you are indeed the All-knowing Buddha, tell me of my past practice of virtue so that I may know.

Brahma, you once gave water to many people who were exhausted and thirsty due to the intense heat of the sun. I remember that past practice of virtue of yours, like a man waking from sleep.
164:
You once freed the people who were captured and being led away at the bank of the Eṇī River. I remember that past practice of virtue of yours, like one waking from sleep.

In the current of the Ganges, you once freed a boat that a fierce Naga had seized by force, intending to harm the people. I remember that past practice of virtue of yours, like one waking from sleep.

A disciple named Kappa once lived near you. You did not know that he was wise and endowed with practice (thinking "it is I"). I remember that past practice of virtue of yours, like one waking from sleep.

O Gautama, you truly know the extent of my life. You also know all other Dhammas. Because you know thus, you are called Buddha. Because you are the Buddha, your radiant majesty exists, illuminating the entire Brahma world (so Baka Brahma said).

## The Baka Jātaka is the tenth (Finished).

## The Kukku-vagga is the first (Finished).

The summary of that Vagga is:
Varakaṇṇika Jātaka, the noble Cāpa Jātaka, Sutanu Jātaka, then Gijjha Jātaka, Sarohitamaccha Jātaka, again Paṇṇaka Jātaka, Senaka Jātaka, Yācanaka Jātaka, then Veri Jātaka, together with Brahmabaka Jātaka, there are ten.
165:
## 2. Gandhāra-vagga

## 406. Gandhāra Jātaka (7-2-1)

Ascetic Videha, you have renounced sixteen thousand prosperous villages and flourishing granaries, and now you practice storing (alms food and such).

Teacher, having renounced the Gandhāra kingdom which was full of great wealth and having come out from ruling as a king, why do you now rule and admonish me in this forest?

Ascetic Videha, I speak only the Dhamma; I do not like unrighteousness. To me who speaks the Dhamma, evil demerit cannot cling or smear.

Teacher, if by some reason another person becomes unhappy or disturbed in heart, even if it is of great benefit, a wise person should not speak such words.

Ascetic Videha, whether they get angry or not, or whether they are scattered like a handful of chaff, to me who speaks the Dhamma, evil demerit cannot cling or smear.

If beings did not have their own wisdom or well-trained discipline (Vinaya), many people would wander and act like a blind buffalo in the forest.

Because some in this world have conduct well-trained under a teacher, they, having disciplined Vinaya, live and practice with a well-concentrated mind.

## The Gandhāra Jātaka is finished.

## 407. Mahākapi Jātaka (7-2-2)

O Monkey King, you who made yourself a bridge and let that troop of monkeys cross safely without harm, how are you related to them, and how are they related to you?

O King, subduer of enemies, I am their lord and king, the leader of the troop. For those monkeys who were overwhelmed by sorrow and fear, (I gave up my life).

I made myself leap well and reached a place about a hundred bow-lengths away. From there, I firmly tied a mass of creepers to my hind legs.
166:
Like a cloud torn asunder by the force of the wind, I reached the mango tree. Unable to reach the tree [properly], I grasped a mango branch with both hands.

Stretched out like a bowstring by the mango branch and the rattan vine, the monkeys stepped on me with their feet and crossed safely to the other side.

I was once the king of those sixty thousand monkeys. Because I was able to bring happiness to them, this rattan vine bound to my body does not distress me, nor will death cause me grief.

O Great King, subduer of enemies, this incident is an example for you; please listen and take heed of this instruction. A wise king should seek only the welfare of the kingdom, the vehicles, the army, and all the people of the market towns.

## Mahākapi Jātaka, the Second.

## 408. Kumbhakāra Jātaka (7-2-3)
In the midst of the forest, I saw a mango tree of dark green hue, laden with fruit and flourishing greatly. Later, I saw that very same mango tree broken and ruined because of its fruit. Seeing that destruction, I was moved by spiritual urgency and practiced the life of a monk who wanders for alms.

A woman wore an exceedingly smooth jeweled bracelet fashioned by a wise goldsmith. While there was only one on each arm, there was no sound, but when a second bracelet was added, it began to jingle. Seeing that occurrence, I was moved by spiritual urgency and practiced the life of a monk who wanders for alms.

A bird carrying a piece of meat was attacked by a flock of other birds for the sake of food. Seeing the danger caused by that food, I was moved by spiritual urgency and practiced the life of a monk who wanders for alms.

In the midst of a herd of cattle, I saw a great bull with a swaying hump, endowed with beauty and strength. Later, I saw that very same bull being gored and oppressed because of desire. Seeing that destruction, I was moved by spiritual urgency and practiced the life of a monk who wanders for alms.
167:
King Karaṇḍaka of Kaliṅga, King Naggaji of Gandhāra, King Nimi of Videha, and King Dummukha of Pañcāla—these kings renounced their kingdoms and became monks, possessing nothing.

All these noble ones, like gods, have come together. Just like a blazing fire, these noble ones shine with the virtue of morality. O Bhaggava, I too shall renounce limited sensual pleasures and practice alone.

Now is the time to become a monk; there is no other time. In the future, there will be no one to instruct me. O Bhaggava, I too shall practice alone, like a female bird escaped from a man's hand.

The children know what is raw and what is cooked, as well as what is salty and what is bland. Seeing that occurrence, I have become a monk. You too should practice; I shall practice as well.

## The Kumbhakāra Jātaka is finished.

## 409. Daḷhadhamma Jātaka (7-2-4)

If I, while serving the interests of King Daḷhadhamma, could not please him, (who then could please him?). I moved valiantly in battle and bore arrows and spears in my chest.

Does the king not know of my courage and well-performed deeds in battle, and my missions as a messenger?

Indeed, I, without relatives or refuge, am about to die. At such a time, I have been given to a potter to haul cow dung.

As long as a man desires some benefit, for that long only does he attend [to another]. When the benefit is gone, like a Khattiya king discarding a diseased camel, they discard that person.

Even when there is a favor done in the past, and one's own benefit has been fulfilled by another, the desired prosperity of one who is ungrateful will be destroyed.
168:
If a person, having had a good favor done for them in the past and having had their affairs fulfilled by another, recognizes that gratitude, the desired prosperity of that person will increase and multiply.

O friends gathered here, I say to you: May you all be grateful people. If you are so, you shall remain in the celestial realm for a long time.

## The Daḷhadhamma Jātaka is finished.

## 410. Somadatta Jātaka (7-2-5)

In the past, in the forest, I no longer see that elephant named Somadatta who used to come from afar to welcome me. Where has Somadatta gone?

This elephant lies dead. Like a vine cut and thrown on the sand in the summer, he lies on the ground. Alas, the great tusker is dead!

For a monk like you, who has renounced the world, become a recluse, and is free from defilements, it is not proper to grieve for the deceased.

O Sakka, whether it be a human or an animal, love arises in the heart through living together. One cannot help but grieve for such a loved one.

Those who weep and wail do so for the dead or for those about to die. Therefore, O sage, do not weep. The wise say that weeping is useless.

O sage, if by weeping the dead would come back to life, we would all gather and weep for each other's relatives.

Just as one extinguishes a fire fed with ghee by pouring water on it, you have extinguished all my burning grief.

You have pulled out the thorn of grief that resided in my heart, I who was mourning for my son.

O Sakka, having heard your words, I have pulled out the thorn of grief; I am free from sorrow, my mind is clear, and I no longer grieve or weep.

## The Somadatta Jātaka is finished.
169:
## 411. Susīma Jātaka (7-2-6)
In the past, the hairs on the parts of my head where they grow were dark like the color of a bumblebee. O Susīma, now seeing that these hairs have turned white, I shall practice the Dhamma; it is time to lead the holy life.

Great King, this white hair is mine alone; it is not yours. It is hair that grew on my head, my topmost limb. Thinking to do what is beneficial, I spoke a falsehood; O Great King, please forgive this one offense of mine.

Great King, you are still young and lovely to look upon, like a newly sprouted bamboo shoot. Please continue to rule as king and look after me; O Great King, do not yet enter the state of a monk which yields fruit only later.

I see a young maiden with a smooth complexion in all her limbs, a beautiful body, and a fine waist. Like a creeper swaying in a gentle breeze, she moves about as if enticing men.

Later, I see that same woman, now eighty or ninety years old from birth, walking with a staff, trembling, her body bent like a roof-rafter.

Contemplating repeatedly on the gratification and the danger of that form, I lie alone in the middle of my bed. Seeing that I too must become like this, I no longer delight in the home; it is time to lead the holy life.
170:
The delight of one living in a home is like a rope that binds. The wise, having cut even that delight in the home and abandoned sensual pleasures, depart without longing.

## Susīma Jātaka, the Sixth.

## 412. Koṭasimbali Jātaka (7-2-7)

I have come carrying a Nāga a thousand fathoms long. Even though you have to support me and that Nāga of great body, you do not tremble.

O deity of the silk-cotton tree, seeing this small female bird which has much less flesh than we whom I have brought, what reason do you see for trembling with fear?

O King of Garuḍas, you eat flesh, but this bird eats fruit. This bird, having eaten the seeds of the banyan, the waved-leaf fig, the cluster fig, and the sacred fig, will void its excrement upon my trunk.

The banyan and other trees growing from those seeds will flourish in the windless hollows of my branches. Those trees will entwine me and make me no longer a tree (leaving me no space).

There are other great trees whose roots and trunks have been destroyed because this bird brought seeds to them.

Parasitic plants growing upon a tree flourish by even overcoming the great lord of the forest. Therefore, O King of Garuḍas, I tremble seeing the danger yet to come.

One should dread what is to be dreaded; one should guard against the danger yet to come. The wise person who foresees the danger yet to come is said to look to both worlds, the present and the future.

## Koṭasimbali Jātaka, the Seventh.

## 413. Dhūmakāri Jātaka (7-2-8)

King Koravya, named Yudhiṭṭhila, who desired the Dhamma, questioned the wise Vidhūra: "O Brahmin teacher, do you know who is the one person that grieves much alone?" he asked.
171:
A Brahmin of the Vāseṭṭha clan, while living in the forest with a herd of goats and many cattle, tirelessly made piles of smoke day and night to drive away mosquitoes and flies.

Because of the scent of that smoke, the sarabha deer, tormented by mosquitoes and flies, came to that smoke-making Brahmin to stay for the three months of the rainy season.

That Brahmin, with his mind inclined only toward the sarabha deer and showing them affection, no longer cared for or noticed his own goats. Whether those goats came or went to graze in the forest, he could not protect them, and they were destroyed, being caught and eaten by lions, leopards, and tigers.

When the mosquitoes and flies in the forest disappeared during the month of Kattika, the sarabha deer departed into difficult mountain passes and to the sources of rivers.

When he saw and realized that the sarabha deer had gone and the goats had come to ruin, that Brahmin, having lost both, was tormented by grief, became emaciated and pale, and was afflicted with jaundice.

In this way, whoever discards their original old friends (insiders) and loves only the newly arrived guests, that person, like this Brahmin Dhūmakāri, will grieve greatly alone.

## Dhūmakāri Jātaka, the Eighth.

## 414. Jāgara Jātaka (7-2-9)

Who is asleep among those who are awake? Who is awake among those who are asleep? Who knows this riddle of mine? Who can answer it for me?

I am asleep among those who are awake; I am awake among those who are asleep. I know this riddle; I shall answer it for you.

How are you asleep among those who are awake? How are you awake among those who are asleep? How do you know this riddle? How do you answer me?

O deity, those who do not know the restraint (saṃyama) of the virtue of the path and the self-control (dama) of the virtue of sense-restraint—among those who are heedless and asleep, I am awake.

O deity, for those Arahants in whom lust, hatred, and ignorance have faded away—among those Arahants who are awake, I am asleep.
172:
In the midst of those who are awake, I am asleep; in the midst of those who are asleep, I am awake. Thus do I understand this problem; thus do I answer you.

O ascetic, it is well that you are asleep among the awake, and well that you are awake among the asleep. It is well that you understand my problem; it is well that you can answer it.

## The Jāgara Jātaka is the ninth.

## 415. Kummāsapiṇḍa Jātaka (7-2-10)

Service to the Paccekabuddhas of noble vision is not of little fruit. Behold the fruit of a dry, saltless barley cake.

These many elephants, cattle, and horses, the wealth, grain, and the whole earth, and these women like celestial nymphs—all are the fruits of the gift of barley cake. Behold the fruit of the barley cake.

O King of Kosala, enhancer of the realm, you constantly recite these verses with a very joyful heart. O enhancer of the realm, I ask you: you speak with a heart full of great joy.

In this very city of Vārāṇasī, I was born into an obscure family. I was a laborer working for others, yet I was restrained in virtue.

While going out to work, I saw four Paccekabuddhas, perfected in conduct and virtue, calmed, and free from taints (āsavas).

Having gained faith in them, I invited them to sit on a bed of leaves, and with a devout heart, I gave them barley cakes with my own hands.
174:
My beloved wife, who lives in the village and is beyond reproach, will cause me grief. Just as that branch made Parantapa thin and pale, so will she make me thin and pale.

O lady with dark eyelashes, your smiles and pleasant words will make me thin and pale, just as that branch did to Parantapa.

The sound of that shaking branch has surely reached you. You have surely heard that sound. He who shook that branch has surely told you the reason.

I, a fool, thought that the branch was shaken by a man or a beast. But now, that danger has arrived along with you.

You killed my father in that very way. Having killed my father and covered him with branches, danger shall now come to you.

## The Parantapa Jātaka, the eleventh, is finished.

## The second Gandhara Vagga is finished.

The summary verse of that Vagga is:
Varagāma Jātaka, Mahākapi Jātaka, Bhaggava Jātaka, Daḷhadhamma Jātaka, Sakuñjara Jātaka, Kesava Jātaka, Uraga Jātaka, Vidhura Jātaka, Jāgara Jātaka, Kosalādhipa Jātaka, and Parantapa Jātaka.

The summary of the Vaggas:
In this Sattaka Nipāta, listen to the Vaggas I preach. The Kukku Vagga and the Gandhara Vagga—these two Vaggas were well preached by the Great Sage.

## The Sattaka Nipāta is finished.
175:
## 8. Aṭṭhaka Nipāta
## 417. Kaccāni Jātaka (1)

While the Buddha was staying at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Kaccāni Jātaka concerning a lay follower who supported his mother. At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. Sakka, seeing a poor woman cooking sesame rice in a cemetery, thinking that "Dhamma is dead," approached her in the guise of a Brahmin and asked:

O woman of the Kaccāni lineage, wearing white clothes, pure and clean, with wet hair, why have you placed a pot on a skull as a tripod? You are washing rice with sesame powder. For what reason will there be sesame rice?

O Brahmin, this well-cooked sesame rice is not for eating. The Dhamma of respecting and supporting one's parents and elders has died today. Therefore, I will prepare this food for the dead (matakabhatta) in the middle of the cemetery for that Dhamma.

O woman of the Kaccāni lineage, do what needs to be done after investigating with wisdom. Who told you that Dhamma is dead? The noble Dhamma, which has a thousand eyes of wisdom to see the benefit and has incomparable power, never dies.

O Great Brahmin, my decision regarding the death of Dhamma is firm. I have no doubt about it. Nowadays, only those with evil conduct are happy.

My daughter-in-law was barren before, but now she has beaten me and driven me out after giving birth to a son. That daughter-in-law now rules the whole house, while I, being driven out, live alone in misery.
176:
O Lady of the Kaccāni lineage, I am indeed alive; I am not dead. I have come here only for your benefit. I shall destroy that daughter-in-law, who killed you and gave birth to a son, along with her son, reducing them to ashes.

O King of the Gods, if it pleases you so, let your coming here be only for my benefit. I, my son, my daughter-in-law, and my grandson wish to live in this house in joy and harmony.

O Lady of the Kaccāni lineage, I shall grant your wish. Even though you were killed, you did not abandon the virtue of loving-kindness toward the young ones. Because you did not abandon such virtue, let it be as you desire. I admire this virtue of yours. May you, your son, your daughter-in-law, and your grandson live in this house in joy and harmony.

That woman of the Kaccāni lineage lived in the house in joy and harmony with her daughter-in-law. Having received the favor of Sakka, the King of the Gods, her son and grandson also attended to and cared for her.

## Kaccāni Jātaka, the First.

## 418. Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka (2)

In the past, this auspicious pond was a hollow, full of many fish and abundant water. It was the dwelling of the King of Cranes and also the ancestral home of my parents. Now, although we must subsist only on frogs and are oppressed by hunger, we cannot abandon this place.

Who will pierce the second eye of the immoral mahout named Bandhura? Who will ensure the safety of my sons, our nest, and myself?

O Great King, the existence of that sapwood lasted only so long. All that sapwood has been consumed. The woodworm, whose food is exhausted, no longer finds delight in the heartwood.
177:
When shall I, having been freed from this King’s palace, go and delight myself, making a nest among the tree branches lush with blooming flowers?

When shall I, having been freed from this King’s palace, go and drink the first clear waters, walking at the head of the herd of deer?

I, who was intoxicated by sensual pleasures and infatuated with desires, was captured from the forest by a hunter from the Bāhika country. O King, may good fortune and blessings be upon you.

In the impenetrable darkness upon the high mountain peak, that Kinnarī, with soft and gentle words, held my hand and guided me down, saying, 'Lord, do not slip on the rock.'

I, who see the end of birth (Nibbāna), shall certainly not enter a womb again. This is my final life; this is my last conception. My wandering in Saṃsāra is ended, and there will be no further rebirth.

## Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka, the Second.

## 419. Sulasa Jātaka (3)

O noble sir, may blessings be upon you. Take this golden necklace and these many pearls and gems. Take me also, and proclaim in the midst of the people, 'She is my slave.'

O beautiful lady, take off the ornaments you are wearing; do not weep so bitterly. I have never known myself to take wealth without killing the owner.

From the time I have been self-aware until I reached the age of discretion, I have never known anyone I loved more than you.

Come, let me embrace you and worship you by circumambulating you to the right. From now on, there will be no further meeting between you and me.

It is not only the man who is wise in all situations; a woman too can be wise, being discerning in various matters.
179:
Those kings who delight in the ten royal virtues taught by the righteous kings of old are supreme in word, mind, and deed.

Those righteous kings of such nature, having abandoned bias and being well-established in the peace of defilements, the gentleness (soracca) of noble virtue, and firm concentration (samādhi), proceed to both worlds.

I am the king, the lord of men and women; even if I should become angry, I shall restrain myself with the goad of wisdom and remain established in the Dhamma laid down by the kings of old.

Out of compassion for such people, I shall administer punishment in a proper and just manner.

O Great King, may your retinue and your glory and wisdom never leave you. Being free from anger and always having a clear and devout mind, may you protect [the kingdom] for a hundred years without suffering.

O Great King, being endowed with these virtues, established in the noble conduct of kings, easy to speak to, and free from anger, rule the earth happily without oppressing the beings in your own country, and when you are released from this life, may you go to a happy destination (sugati).

Just as a great rain cloud cools the earth with water, so should one calm the agitated masses through well-conducted reasons, well-spoken words, and the methods of righteous discipline.

## Sumangala Jātaka, the Fourth.

## 421. Gangamāla Jātaka (5)

The earth is like glowing coals without flame; this ground is like hot sand that has become hot ashes. Yet, you wear your ascetic garments and sing; does the heat of the sun not burn you?

Above, the sun burns; below, the sand burns. Yet, you wear your ascetic garments and sing; does the heat of the sun not burn you?
180:
O Great King, the heat of the sun and the earth does not burn me. Only the desires of the senses (vatthu-kāma) and the defilement of lust (kilesa-kāma) burn me. Indeed, the affairs and duties that arise depending on desire are many and various. Only those matters burn me; the heat of the sun and the earth does not burn me.

O Desire (kāma), I have seen your root. O Desire, you are born of thought. I shall no longer think of you. O Desire, if I do not think of you in this way, you will no longer arise within me.

Even a small amount of sensual objects and desires is not enough for people. Even with many desires, people cannot be satisfied. A person who cleanses impurities with wakeful effort should abandon these desires, which cause the foolish to say 'this is mine' and which should not be clung to.

This benefit is the result of my small wholesome deed. I, who am named Udaya, have reached great prosperity and happiness. For that young man who, having abandoned sensual lust, has become a monk, the attainment of human existence is indeed a good attainment.

Beings abandon evil deeds through ascetic virtue (tapasā). Through ascetic virtue, they abandon the state of being a barber or a potter. Gangamāla, is it appropriate for a barber like you to now oppress my son with your virtue and address him by the name 'Brahmadatta'?

Mother, behold this visible fruit of patience (khantī) and virtue (soracca). We, the king and the ministers, pay homage to that Paccekabuddha who is worthy of the homage of all people.

Friends, do not say anything at all to Gangamāla, who is striving in the practice of the sages (muni). For he has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra, which the sorrow-free Noble Ones cross and travel beyond.

## Gangamāla Jātaka, the Fifth.

## 422. Cetiya Jātaka (6)

O Great King, indeed, the Dhamma (Truth/Justice) that is destroyed kills the one who destroys it. The Dhamma that is not destroyed does not kill anyone. Therefore, one should not destroy the Dhamma; let not the destroyed Dhamma kill you in return.
181:
The deities depart from one who speaks falsehood; his mouth smells of rot, and he falls from his position—he who, knowing the truth, when asked a question, explains it otherwise. O King, if you speak the truth, be as you were before; O King, if you speak a lie, remain [sunk] in the earth, Cetiya.

In the country of that person who, knowing the truth, when asked a question, explains it otherwise, it rains out of season, and in season it does not rain. O King, if you speak the truth, be as you were before; O King, if you speak a lie, enter into the earth, Cetiya.

O King, Lord of the Directions, the tongue of that person who, knowing the truth, when asked a question, explains it otherwise, becomes forked like a snake's tongue. O King, if you speak the truth, be as you were before; O King, if you speak a lie, enter further into the earth, Cetiya.

O King, Lord of the Directions, the tongue of that person who, knowing the truth, when asked a question, explains it otherwise, becomes non-existent like a fish's tongue. O King, if you speak the truth, be as you were before; O King, if you speak a lie, enter further into the earth, Cetiya.

In the family of that person who, knowing the truth, when asked a question, explains it otherwise, only daughters are born; sons are not born. O King, if you speak the truth, be as you were before; O King, if you speak a lie, enter further into the earth, Cetiya.

That person who, knowing the truth, when asked a question, explains it otherwise, has no sons; they depart in all directions. O King, if you speak the truth, be as you were before; O King, if you speak a lie, enter further into the earth, Cetiya.
182:
That King Cetiya, cursed by the ascetic, though formerly able to travel through the air, fell into the earth when his turn to die arrived, because of his base nature. Therefore, the wise do not praise following the path of favoritism (chandāgati); one should speak words associated with truth, with a mind not corrupted by favoritism and the like.

## Cetiya Jātaka is finished.

## 423. Indriya Jātaka (7)

O Nārada, he who follows the dictates of the senses through the power of sensual desire, having abandoned both worlds, withers away even while alive.

Suffering follows immediately after happiness; happiness follows immediately after suffering. You too have reached suffering from happiness; look forward again to the highest happiness.

The wise person who is able to endure in times of hardship and does not succumb to the power of suffering but overcomes it, that wise one shall reach happiness (yoga), which is the end of suffering.

One should not fall away from the Dhamma because of desiring sensual pleasures, nor because of wishing to avoid harm or seeking benefit. Having destroyed the attained (jhāna) states, one should not deviate from the Dhamma.

For householders, being energetic is good; sharing food is good; not being ostentatious (not being heedless) when gaining wealth, and being unshaken when wealth is lost, are indeed excellent.

The ascetic Devila spoke these words of wisdom. There is no one more base than he who follows the dictates of the senses.

I have reached destruction as if I had fallen into the hands of enemies. Having lost my retinue and fame—work, knowledge, skill, marriage, virtue, and gentleness—it has happened because of my own deeds.

I, without kin and without refuge, having departed from the Noble Dhamma, am just like a hungry ghost (peta).
183:
Because I caused suffering to beings who desired happiness, I have reached this mass of suffering. I, standing as if surrounded by fires and burning, can no longer find happiness.

## Indriya Jātaka, the seventh.

## 424. Āditta Jātaka (8)

Just as an article rescued from a house that is blazing brightly is for the benefit of the householder, and not that which is burnt therein.

In the same way, the world is set ablaze by the fires of aging and death. Therefore, one should rescue one's wealth through giving (dāna); only that which is given is truly rescued wealth.

The being who gives a gift obtained righteously and acquired through energetic effort, crosses the Vaitaraṇī river of King Yama and reaches the celestial realms of the devas.

The wise say that giving and fighting a battle are similar. Just as a few soldiers, disregarding their lives, can defeat many, if one gives even a small gift with faith in kamma and its results, through that very gift, one reaches happiness in the next world.

The Buddha praises the gift given after careful selection. In this world of the living, there are those worthy of offerings; gifts given to them are of great fruit, like seeds sown in a good field.

He who practices without harming beings does no evil for fear of others' blame. The virtuous praise him who fears the blame of others; in such a case, they do not praise the one who is bold and fearless. The virtuous do no evil because they fear blame.

Through a low practice of the holy life (brahmacariya), one is born into a royal family. Through a medium practice, one reaches the state of a deva. Through the highest practice, one is purified from the round of suffering of the defilements.
184:
Indeed, giving (dāna) is praised in many ways, but the collection of Dhamma (calm, insight, path, and fruition) is superior to giving. In this Bhadda-kappa, the virtuous ones such as Kassapa Buddha who appeared formerly, and the wise virtuous ones such as Vessabhū Buddha who appeared in even earlier aeons, having developed calm and insight, reached only Nibbāna.

## Āditta Jātaka, the eighth.

## 425. Aṭṭhāna Jātaka (9)

Sister, when the Ganges River remains still without flowing, covered with white lotuses; when cuckoos have a white color like a conch shell; and when the rose-apple tree bears palmyra fruit; only in such a time could our union be possible.

When there are three kinds of garments woven from tortoise hair, and there is a cloak suitable for wrapping in winter; only in such a time could I truly be united with you.

When a watchtower well-constructed from the legs of gnats and mosquitoes is firm and unshakable; only in such a time could I truly be united with you.

When there is a ladder well-constructed from rabbit horns for ascending to the celestial realm; only in such a time could I truly be united with you.

When mice climb a ladder and bite the moon, and drive away Rāhu; only in such a time could I truly be united with you.

When flies that roam in swarms drink from a liquor jar and, becoming intoxicated, dwell upon glowing coals; only in such a time could I truly be united with you.

When a donkey with a beautiful face and lips red like a ripe ivy gourd is skilled in dancing and singing; only in such a time could I truly be united with you.

When crows and owls consult in a secret place and, desiring each other's prosperity, protect one another; only in such a time could I truly be united with you.

When an umbrella made of lotus stalks and leaves is very strong for protection against rain; only in such a time could I truly be united with you.
185:
When a small kulaṅka bird carries Mount Gandhamādana in its beak and flies away, only then might there truly be an association between us.

When a servant boy lifts up an ocean-going ship along with its equipment and flies away, only then might there truly be an association between us.

## The Aṭṭhāna Jātaka is the ninth.

## 426. Dīpi Jātaka (10)
"Uncle, are you healthy? Are you comfortable and at ease? Is it well with you, Uncle? My mother sends her greetings for your well-being; we only desire your happiness."

"She-goat, you came here after treading on my tail and harassing me. Do you think that today you shall be released merely by calling me 'Uncle'?"

"Uncle, you are sitting facing the East, and I approached from your front. How could I possibly have trodden on your tail which is behind you?"

"She-goat, as far as the four great islands extend, together with the oceans and mountains, so far does my tail reach. How could you have avoided it?"

"My parents and brothers told me before that the tail of a wicked panther is long. Therefore, I approached through the air."

"She-goat, seeing you coming through the air, the herd of animals fled. You have destroyed my prey."

While the she-goat was thus lamenting, the flesh-eating panther bit and crushed her throat. In one who is wicked, well-spoken words have no effect.
186:
In a wicked person, there is no logic, no Dhamma, and no well-spoken word. One should only exert effort to escape from a wicked person; such a person does not delight in the words of the virtuous.

## The tenth Dīpi Jātaka is finished.

## The Book of the Eights (Aṭṭhakanipāta) is finished.

The summary of this Aṭṭhakanipāta is:
Parisuddhā, Manāvilā, Vatthadharā,
Bakarājā, Kāyura, Daṇḍavara,
Then Aṅgāra, Cetiya, Devilinā,
Then Āditta, Gaṅgā, and the tenth, Eḷikinā.
